articles.title: Thousands of flights canceled as airlines work to dig out from nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Airlines across the U. worked to recover from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years that canceled more than 2,500 flights Saturday...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Airlines across the U.S. worked to recover from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years that canceled more than 2,500 flights Saturday, spread ripple effects around the world, stranded passengers and forced pro and college sports teams to scramble for alternate transportation.

New technology being added to the nation's air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused "intermittent" communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, Trump administration officials said.

Airports were slowly returning to normal, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said, with planes taking flight and landing. But the effects could be felt for days, with officials saying the system would likely return to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.

The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023 , when another key Federal Aviation Administration computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said the stoppage on Friday had affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day.

"The knock-on effect of that is incredible," said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. "The aircraft doesn't just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you're talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific."

Thousands of flights delayed and canceled

At airports across the U.S., passengers stared at screens showing delays or rushed to find buses or trains to their destinations.

Emily Brown and her 14-year-old daughter waited more than four hours Friday at the Dallas airport for their flight to Columbus, Ohio, before giving up. They were traveling to surprise her daughter's best friend. Instead, she had to settle for phoning the friend through tears in the airport, Brown said.

"She saved up her money to buy her own ticket, and she's planned this whole weekend," Brown said. "Now we're not sure when we're gonna be able to go."

A cheerful Southwest Airlines gate agent greeted passengers at Dallas Love Field at dawn Saturday with "Good morning, good morning," but then repeatedly said all flights were full and asked passengers to have boarding passes ready to expedite the process and help keep flights moving.

Sports teams scheduled to play this weekend adjusted game start times, searched for hotel rooms, rescheduled flights and chartered buses.

Auburn University's football team opted to take a bus to Mississippi State and the Saturday start time was pushed back from noon ET to 4:15 p.m. Other universities affected by the stoppage included Baylor, Washington, Kansas State, Minnesota and No. 19 Ole Miss, which did not plan to fly until Saturday morning for its game against Oklahoma.

More than 2,500 flights were canceled in the U.S. Saturday and hundreds more were delayed, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.

Corbyn Wascher's flight was on the tarmac at Charlotte Douglas International Airport for four hours Friday on his way home to Moline, Illinois, from a conference in Miami. The 37-year-old high school teacher paid $100 to take an Uber to a hotel 25 minutes from the airport after he was unable to find a flight until Saturday afternoon to Chicago O'Hare International Airport.

At London's Heathrow Airport, several flights to and from the U.S. were listed as delayed or canceled Saturday, including American Airlines flights to Dallas and Los Angeles, and a British Airways flight to New York's JFK Airport. A Delta flight from Atlanta, an American flight from Miami and a United flight from Chicago were also listed as canceled.

"While U.S. flights have resumed, there may be some follow-on disruption as airlines work to rebook affected passengers and get all services back to normal," said Tim Johnson, consumer director at the U.K. Civil Aviation Authority.

Officials say no one was in danger during ground stop

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely Friday.

Duffy blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He suggested more disruptions might occur.

"We didn't think we would have this kind of outage. We did," he said. "We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these."

Duffy said the failure Friday involved old equipment and was not linked to the FAA's new AI-powered system, which the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky.

The problem was due to updating a system that can never shut down, Charlton said.

"What you're watching here is trying to change the tires of your car when the car's going at 80 miles an hour down the expressway, because nothing stops in aviation," Charlton said. "It's a 24/7 operation. And to make changes on the fly, if you'll pardon that pun, is incredibly complex and dangerous."

The FAA has already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.

Past problems have been linked to equipment failures

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport .

Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time was the nationwide scale of the disruption, which left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.

"If you don't have that ability, whether it's because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you've got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you're going to risk not being able to communicate with them," said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.

Friday's ground stop also differed from the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.

Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska, and Golden from Seattle. Associated Press journalists David Keaton in Berlin; Stephen Hawkins in Dallas; Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Jessica Hill in Las Vegas; Ali Swenson in Chicago; Alex Veiga and Jaimie Ding in Los Angeles; Seung Min Kim and Aamer Madhani in Washington; Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City; and Brian Melley in London contributed to this report.

articles.title: US to resume flights after air traffic network failure sparks chaos
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The FAA lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday after a communications failure at air traffic control centers caused chaos a...
articles.body:
By David Shepardson, Doyinsola Oladipo and Rajesh Kumar Singh

WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The FAA lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday after a communications failure at air traffic control centers caused chaos at US airports and triggered the longest shutdown since the September 11, 2001, attacks.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said US airspace reopened ‌at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time (0115 GMT), but warned that departures would resume gradually and it would take time for airlines to restore normal operations.

"It's going to be slow," Duffy ‌told reporters at the White House.

By 11:30 p.m., nearly 10,000 flights had been canceled, including more than 2,200 each at Delta Air Lines and American Airlines, and 1,800 at United Airlines, according to Flightradar24. The plane-tracking website said some ​aircraft at major airports had waited more than five hours for a gate.

The four-hour nationwide grounding could disrupt airline schedules for days, aviation analysts said.

Duffy said tens of thousands of passengers were stranded at airports around the country. Duffy said he and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had met with President Donald Trump in the Oval Office to discuss the outage.

The failure is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by aging technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several thousand controllers.

Duffy said the trouble began at 3:36 p.m., when air ‌traffic control centers experienced instability in radar and communications systems.

"Our switches, ⁠our routers actually got overloaded with data and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data from those routers and because of that we shut the system down," Duffy said, adding that at no stage did they completely lose radar or communications and they were able to safely land ⁠thousands of planes.

Duffy said the immediate problem had been fixed and that flying was safe, but warned that a broader overhaul of the aging air traffic control system was needed to prevent similar failures.

Duffy blamed Congress not funding a new system that he said could prevent such outages, and called for $50 billion to modernize it.

Earlier on Friday, before the outage, the White House and Department of Transportation had ​urged ​Congress to approve $30.1 billion to upgrade the nation's aging airports and air traffic control infrastructure.

"What we have is an ​incredibly old air traffic control system," Duffy said. "Give us the money to ‌fix it."

articles.title: Jordi Wild reacciona a su ruleta de entrevistas con Sánchez, Feijóo y Colau: "Y por supuesto, he cometido fallos"
articles.standfirst: El youtuber hace su propio análisis a última hora del día sobre lo acontecido con las entrevistas
articles.summary: El youtuber hace su propio análisis a última hora del día sobre lo acontecido con las entrevistas
articles.body: Jordi Wild fue el protagonista de la jornada de ayer en el primer día de campaña electoral con sus entrevistas a los principales líderes políticos de España menos el consabido de Santiago Abascal que declinó la invitación finalmente. El youtuber tuvo una mañana intensa. Muchas preguntas, mucho análisis con Pedro Sánchez, Alberto Núñez Feijóo y Ada Colau y dejó pasar la tarde para ver las reacciones. Pero a última hora de la tarde llegó la reacción de Wild y lo hizo a través de las redes sociales para dejar su opinión de cómo había trascendido todo. Lo primero que dejó caer: "Mil gracias a todos por las muestras de cariño por estas entrevistas, siempre es bonito ver que tu trabajo es recompensado así", expresó en clave de reconocimiento a todo el mundo. A su vez el propio Wild dejó constancia de autocrítica. De análisis por lo hecho y de reflexión. Y reconoció claramente y sin ningún rubor: "Y por supuesto, he cometido fallos". Él mismo explicaba, en clave de conclusión, que "en fin, que tomo nota de mis errores, y he aprendido de estas charlas para hacerlo mucho mejor en el futuro. Aunque, la verdad, estoy muy orgulloso y contento de cómo han ido. Para ser la primera vez que hago algo así, no está mal". "La verificación en directo fue complicada de coordinar, es algo lento, y cuando me pasaban información, yo ya estaba dos temas más allá. Y encima, a veces se me olvidaba revisarlo, al tener que estar pendiente de la conversación y del invitado. Si vuelvo a hacer algo así, creo que sería bueno tener a otro periodista ahí en la mesa, SOLO para coordinar verificaciones, y yo poder centrarme en charlar", señalaba el propio Wild. "Plantear 4 entrevistas así tan intensas en 4 días seguidos fue una mala idea. Comencé con mucha energía en la primera (Colau), y en la última (Feijóo) estaba drenado y mucho más saturado mentalmente, aunque intentaba que no se me notara. Además, el día anterior con todo lo que pasó, tenía la cabeza como un bombo. Hubiera sido mejor hacer 2 una semana, y 2 la otra. Y publicar así", indicó. "Con Feijóo, gestioné mal el tiempo. Fue con diferencia la charla más corta y me quedaron muchos temas, sobretodo jodidos, fuera: su incomprensible defensa a Mazón, la gestión de las residencias en la pandemia, Angrois, vivienda, Israel... Intenté apretar al final, pero me di cuenta demasiado tarde de que se me terminaba el tiempo, y ellos fueron claros en que tenían que irse. Y estaban en su derecho por las normas que puse (60min mínimo)", explicó el youtuber.

articles.title: Blue wave meets ballot box surprises as voters split on abortion, voter ID and billionaire taxes
articles.summary: Voters in three states approved voter ID measures, while California rejected a billionaire wealth tax and Idaho turned down a proposal to expand abortion rights.
articles.body: While Democrats’ midterm sweep dominated Election Night, voters in several states delivered consequential — and sometimes crosscutting — verdicts on voter ID, abortion access, taxes and English-language laws. But the down-ballot decisions largely unfolded beneath the shadow of the GOP’s crushing losses, offering a separate look at the policy priorities voters chose to elevate in their states. Read on to learn more about some of the most significant ballot measure results that will be shaping the lives of thousands of Americans. New voter ID voting requirements DEMOCRATS ‘DIVORCED FROM VOTERS’ AS 5 STATES BACK CITIZEN-ONLY VOTING, BOLSTERING GOP PUSH Voters in Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio all voted to pass voter ID requirements, even as talks among federal lawmakers have stalled on the issue, showcasing that the issue remains a point of public interest. In North Carolina, the state has required photo ID for in-person voting since 2018. But with the adoption of a constitutional amendment in a 59.6% to 40.3% vote, the Tar Heel State expanded the requirement to all forms of voting. Similarly, in Ohio, voters passed Issue 3 in a 65.3% to 34.6% vote. Although Ohio already had pre-existing in-person voter-ID laws, Issue 3 codified the requirement in the state’s constitution, making it harder to overturn later. Finally, in Nevada, Question 7 passed in a 62.1% to 37.8% vote, establishing a constitutional amendment to enact the state’s first voter-ID requirement. It compels voters to show ID when voting in person and, for mail and absentee ballots, asks voters to provide the last four digits of their driver's license or Social Security number. English is the official language of Idaho EVERYTHING TO KNOW ABOUT HOUSE AND SENATE CONTROL, BALLOT MEASURES AND 2026 ELECTION DAY POLL CLOSING In Idaho, voters approved HJR6 in a 63.1% to 36.8% outcome, a measure that makes English the official language of the state, codifying it for use in public proceedings with a constitutional amendment. English had already been made Idaho’s official language through statute since 2007. State Rep. Dale Hawkins, one of the champions behind HJR6, called it reflective of efforts from the Trump administration to make English the official language of the United States through executive order. "Our current administration signed an executive order doing this for the entire United States so we are just in line with what’s going on," Hawkins said in public remarks. In an interview with local media, Hawkins also cited a concern that many newcomers to the U.S. had, in his view, overlooked the country’s linguistic identity. "One of the things that unites us all as a culture, as a country, as a state, is language. And what used to be the desired effect, which was assimilation — learn the language, learn the culture, learn the history — those things have slipped away. And we don’t see assimilation anymore. And I believe that if we have a common language, then our culture will survive," Hawkins told the Idaho Capital Sun. Voters reject a ‘viability’ right to abortion DEM GOV MAURA HEALEY SIGNS SWEEPING MASSACHUSETTS BILL ALLOWING ABORTIONS UP TO BIRTH Alongside their English language constitutional amendment, voters in Idaho rejected Proposition 1, which would have created a right to abortion up to the point of fetal viability, except in cases of medical emergency. In the words of the proposition itself, it "would support creating a right to abortion before fetal viability—defined as a fetus’ ability to survive without extraordinary medical measures—and after fetal viability in cases of medical emergency; providing protections against professional discipline and civil and criminal liability for healthcare providers; and codifying a statutory reproductive right to freedom and privacy." Proposition 1 failed in a 44.0% to 55.9% outcome. Had it been successful, the measure would have greatly reduced the state’s current limits on abortion except to save the life of a pregnant woman or in cases of rape or incest. To onlookers like Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, the outcome demonstrates that protecting life in the womb remains a priority and an ongoing contest at the state level. "We are incredibly grateful for Stop Prop 1 and all who stood up to defend the unborn. This is a hard-fought win and an example to pro-life voters, candidates and elected officials across the country… Voters were not fooled because pro-life leaders spoke up boldly to expose this initiative," Dannenfelser said in a statement. Socialist-backed 5% tax for billionaires goes up in smoke STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE In California, voters rejected the implementation of a 5% billionaire tax that carried the backing of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The measure, Proposition 40, failed in a 47.5% to 52.4% loss. The proposition would have applied a 5% tax on assets like businesses, securities, art, collectibles and intellectual property while excluding select pensions, real estate and retirement accounts. To prevent billionaires from simply leaving the state, Proposition 40 was designed to retroactively apply to billionaires who were residents of California on Jan. 1, 2026. The DSA framed the measure as a way to distribute wealth and as a kind of scaled-up version of a progressive tax, a tax that scales relative to income. "We have the money in California to pay for the quality schools and healthcare that we need. It just needs to be transferred from the wrong pockets to the right ones. We can do that by taxing the rich," the slideshow reads. Notably, Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed Proposition 40, arguing that it would lessen California’s competitiveness relative to other states. California rejects voter ID Alongside Proposition 40, voters in California also rejected Proposition 39 — a proposed constitutional amendment that would have required ID for in-person voting and checks for the state’s voter registration lists. Like Nevada's Question 7, it also would have asked absentee voters to provide the last four digits of a unique government-issued ID number before securing a mail-in ballot. The measure failed in a 39.4% to 60.5% vote. Ahead of Election Day, Gov. Newsom characterized Proposition 39 as an extension of efforts to restrict access to voting rights. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Trump and his MAGA allies tried to rig our elections once, and California voters shut them down with Prop 50. Prop 39 is just their latest attempt to silence us, because they know they can’t win in California in a fair fight. It’s voter suppression, full stop, and Californians will vote it down in November," Newsom said in a statement.

articles.title: Massie's push to impeach Hegseth splits constituents in his own backyard: 'Pure spite'
articles.summary: Northern Kentucky residents offer sharply divided takes on Thomas Massie's push to impeach Pete Hegseth over the Iran war and his true motives.
articles.body: KENTON COUNTY, Ky. — Rep. Thomas Massie's push to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war drew sharply different reactions from northern Kentucky residents interviewed by Fox News Digital, who offered competing assessments of the outgoing Republican congressman — and whether his latest confrontation with the Trump administration reflects principle or political payback. Fox News Digital visited Covington, the population center of Massie’s district, along with Newport, Erlanger and other communities across the river from Cincinnati, to ask residents about their outgoing congressman and his efforts to impeach the Pentagon chief. Richard Hassebrock, a Covington resident who said he has not always agreed with Massie, welcomed the impeachment effort. "I'm not always a huge fan of Thomas Massie, but on this point I am," Hassebrock told Fox News Digital. TRUMP DEFENDS PENTAGON CHIEF AS MASSIE TARGETS HIM: 'HEGSETH SHOULD BE PRAISED, NOT IMPEACHED' Craig Cuskey, who works in the Covington area but lives just outside the bounds of Massie’s district in Louisville, described the impeachment push as "pure spite" and "petty," saying his opinion of the congressman had deteriorated. The contrasting reactions came after House Republicans voted to refer Massie's impeachment effort against Hegseth to committee, adding another confrontation to the Kentucky Republican's long-running disagreements with President Donald Trump and his party's leadership. Democrats poised to take the gavel in January, however, signaled they will likely take up Massie’s mantle and seek the Pentagon chief’s impeachment. Hassebrock said he was disappointed by Massie's electoral defeat and praised the congressman's independence. "He stands up for himself, he stands up to what he believes in, he's got principles unlike 99% of the other congress people out there," he said. Rilla, a Fort Wright resident who provided only her first name, offered a more complicated assessment. "I think he's just trying to get back at Trump," she said, while adding that she had been proud of Massie for standing up to the president and was disappointed by his defeat. 7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS Rilla said she opposed the Iran war, particularly the prospect of military action without congressional involvement. "I don't think anyone should just go in and declare war without Congress being a part of it," she said. Phil Wiseman, an Independence resident, said he doubted the impeachment effort would accomplish much, even as he questioned the administration's military strategy. "I don't see a definable outcome," Wiseman said. "And if you're going to fight a war, there needs to be a definable outcome." Wiseman said he identifies as a "RINO" — a term often used derisively by conservatives for "Republican in Name Only" — and voted for an independent instead of supporting Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, the Trump-endorsed Republican who defeated Massie in Kentucky's primary earlier this year. He said his family has discussed Hegseth, noting that his father was a 27-year military veteran and his son served in the Marine Corps. "We all had the same discussion," he said. "Who is advising him? Because this [war] is very ill-thought-out and not well-planned." Wiseman compared that aspect of the Iran conflict to how the U.S. previously became mired in Afghanistan. "So I seriously question the military advisors that are giving them this advice, or maybe they gave them contrary advice and it was ignored," he said. Anthony Tuemler of Covington supported impeachment and accused Hegseth of violating the Constitution through his conduct of the war. Tuemler's assessment of Massie was similarly mixed. Although he said he was glad the congressman was leaving office, he credited Massie with speaking up when he believed it was necessary. "I'm glad he's gone," Tuemler said of Massie. "But the only thing I'm distressed about or sorry about is like when it came time to say the right things, Massie was the one who did it." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Randall Thompson of Newport, dressed in a military uniform for Veterans Day as he walked with his children near Covington's Mainstrasse Village corridor, said he supports the defense secretary and pointed to their shared military experience in the Middle East. "I support the troops and Pete Hegseth," Thompson said, adding off-camera that he was in the same area of Iraq as the former Fox News host when they were both deployed. Cuskey also defended Hegseth, saying he had initially been skeptical of his nomination but had grown more impressed with his performance. "I think for his background, he's done a remarkable job," Cuskey said, arguing that Hegseth was carrying out directives from the commander in chief. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has voiced support for impeaching the Pentagon chief, while other Democrats have signaled plans to revisit his conduct when they take control of Congress in January. Some lawmakers are also eyeing investigations and potential impeachment proceedings involving other senior Trump administration officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and border czar Tom Homan — setting the stage for a broader confrontation between congressional Democrats and the White House.

articles.title: Democrats seize on midterm wins to push massive minimum wage hikes, but economists see trouble ahead
articles.summary: Josh Shapiro says he wants to more than double Pennsylvania's minimum wage and codify abortion rights with the new Democratic trifecta.
articles.body: Democrats are pushing major minimum-wage increases after their midterm victories, but economists warn the proposals could come with unintended consequences for small businesses and inexperienced workers. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is pledging to more than double his state's $7.25 minimum wage, while Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is calling for a federal increase as Democrats make affordability a central part of their governing agenda. The renewed push comes as Seattle, which has one of the nation's highest minimum wages, faces concerns about rising business costs and employment opportunities — raising questions about the tradeoffs of higher wage mandates. "We’re going to more than double Pennsylvania‘s minimum wage," Shapiro wrote in an X post this month. "Codify abortion rights into our state Constitution. Fund mass transit. Build more housing. These are the commonsense things that Pennsylvanians want done." AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI "And with a Democratic trifecta, we will deliver on all of them," he continued. Shapiro's proposal would raise Pennsylvania's minimum wage from $7.25 to $15 an hour, an increase of roughly 107%, prompting questions about how small businesses would absorb the additional labor costs. Tom Savidge, an economist with the American Institute for Economic Research, warned in an interview with Fox News Digital that steep wage increases could force small businesses to raise prices, reduce workers' hours or cut back on hiring. "A federal minimum wage hike will worsen the affordability crisis," Savidge told Fox News Digital. "A one-size-fits-all mandate ignores regional differences in wages and business costs. It risks higher prices, fewer hours, and fewer jobs, especially for inexperienced workers. Politicians can mandate higher wages, but they cannot mandate that businesses can afford to pay them." "Small businesses employing minimum-wage workers cannot absorb such a sharp increase without adjusting elsewhere," he added. "Some may raise prices, cut hours, or stop hiring. A higher minimum wage means little to workers who cannot find a job." The debate comes as Democrats seek to deliver on campaign promises to make life more affordable, even as businesses in cities with higher minimum wages report growing financial pressures. Seattle, where the minimum wage is currently $21.30 an hour and will rise to $22.14 in January, offers one example of the economic questions surrounding such policies. While proponents have asserted that minimum wage increases will be a boon to employees, some Seattle business owners have previously raised concerns about facing additional cost burdens, KOMO News reported in December 2025. Rising labor costs have been among the financial pressures cited by Seattle restaurant owners who have closed locations, alongside higher food prices, declining customer demand and other operating expenses, Fox News Digital previously reported. A January survey by The Intentionalist found that 67% of 136 independent small businesses surveyed in Seattle and surrounding Washington communities reported greater financial strain than during the pandemic, with respondents pointing to rising labor costs, rent, insurance and weaker customer demand. A 2022 study published in the American Economic Journal: Economic Policy found that Seattle's 2015 and 2016 minimum-wage increases boosted pay for longer-tenured workers but reduced hours worked, particularly among less-experienced employees, and limited opportunities for people entering low-wage jobs. However, a separate 2017 study by University of California, Berkeley researchers found that Seattle's earlier minimum-wage increases raised wages in the food-service industry without a statistically significant decline in restaurant employment. Savidge went on to say that steep minimum wage increases often benefit major corporations over Main Street businesses. "Higher minimum wages can favor big corporations over small businesses," he explained. "Large corporations can spread higher labor costs across more sales, invest in automation, or relocate operations. Small businesses have fewer options." FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE Despite concerns about the potential economic consequences, Shapiro has made raising Pennsylvania's minimum wage one of his first priorities after Democrats won control of both chambers of the state legislature. "Half a million workers in Pennsylvania still make less than $15 an hour — you can’t live off of that in 2026," Shapiro said. "Now, we’re finally able to change that. The very first bill that I will sign into law with our new Democratic majority this January will be to raise our minimum wage — and make sure every Pennsylvania worker has a livable wage. It’s long overdue." His comments come after Democrats secured a trifecta in Harrisburg in the 2026 midterms after flipping the Pennsylvania state Senate. $25 AN HOUR? MAJOR CITIES EYE MASSIVE WAGE HIKES AS LABOR ACTIVISTS SEEK FEDERAL MANDATE When reached for comment, Shapiro's office referred Fox News Digital to the governor’s comments on raising the minimum wage during an interview with former CNN host Don Lemon released on Sunday. "Some of your some of your viewers and listeners are going to think it's crazy, but job number one is going to be raise the minimum wage to 15 bucks an hour, and now your listeners like, 'What do you mean 15 bucks an hour?'" Shapiro said during the interview. "Everybody's at 15 bucks an hour. Well, we're not in Pennsylvania. We've been stuck at $7.25 an hour for decades, right? Because the Republicans in the state senate, every time we've sent a bill over there, have blocked it." The minimum-wage push is also gaining traction beyond Pennsylvania. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who signed legislation in 2019 gradually raising his state's minimum wage to $15 an hour, is now calling on Congress to increase the federal minimum wage as part of his post-election economic agenda. "Americans made their voices heard and this is an opportunity for Congress to immediately address the challenges of working people – higher wages, lower costs, rooting out corruption," Pritzker said in a statement. "The people of Illinois cannot afford to wait." AOC-BACKED $25 MINIMUM WAGE PLAN SOUNDS GREAT — BUT AT WHAT COST? Savidge told Fox News Digital that Pritzker and Shapiro's minimum wage proposals "risk giving large corporations a competitive advantage while squeezing out smaller competitors." Critics question whether higher wage mandates translate into better overall economic outcomes, particularly for workers with little job experience. Adam Gorcyca, a policy researcher at the Illinois Policy Institute, warned that employers may respond to higher labor costs by reducing hours, limiting hiring or raising prices. "Mandating higher wages doesn't immediately guarantee workers will take home more money," Gorcyca added. "Employers often respond to these policies by cutting back hours, slowing hiring or raising prices. It can help select workers, while also making it harder for entry-level or younger workers." Gorcyca also questioned whether Illinois' minimum-wage increases had delivered broader employment gains, pointing to the state's slow pandemic recovery as evidence of its economic struggles. "In Illinois, Gov. J.B. Pritzker passed a minimum wage hike in 2019, slowly increasing the state’s minimum wage to $15 an hour by 2025," he said. "While he has campaigned that it was the ‘right thing to do,’ the state doesn’t have a stronger labor market for workers. In fact, Illinois was one of the slowest to recover from the pandemic." Pritzker's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on Tuesday. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The push is also emerging as a priority for congressional Democrats. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Monday that the federal minimum wage needs to be raised and that he plans to discuss the issue with members of both chambers of Congress. "It's a conversation that I look forward to having with not simply the members of the House Democratic caucus, but with the Senate as well, to see what is possible," Jeffries said. "It certainly needs to be increased. It's a disgrace that the minimum wage hasn't been raised in 20 years and is currently $7.25 per hour."

articles.title: Socialist LA mayor's bold homelessness promise ahead of 2028 Olympics hit with reality check: 'Not optimistic'
articles.summary: Los Angeles mayor-elect Nithya Raman pledges to halve homeless encampments before the 2028 Olympics, but a local activist warns it won't work.
articles.body: Incoming Los Angeles Mayor Nithya Raman has promised to cut the number of people sleeping in tents and homeless encampments by at least 50% before the 2028 Summer Olympics, but one local activist believes her vision may not be realistic. The blue city’s growing homeless population became a major focus of Raman’s mayoral campaign. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), she plans to expand shelter and housing options while stretching "every dollar as far as possible." John Alle, a business owner and co-founder of the Santa Monica Coalition, told Fox News Digital Raman won’t be able to "hide" the city’s homelessness problem from tourists arriving for the Games and raised concerns about potential gaps in in her plan to deliver lasting results. "I don't think we're going to be able to hide that before the crowds," Alle said, adding that the city has become a "third-world country." 4 OF NATION'S LARGEST CITIES NOW LED BY SOCIALIST MAYORS AFTER TUESDAY'S ELECTION, AFFECTING TENS OF MILLIONS "We're not hiding it now. We're seeing tourists being attacked in Santa Monica, we're seeing tourists being attacked in LA. Our tourism, everything that funds our general fund, our retail sales taxes are all down. The morale of the police, which we need, is down." Alle warned that Raman’s plan will be a temporary solution that will have homeless people moved off the streets ahead of the Olympics and returning once the Games are over. "When the Olympics come, they'll be picked up, they'll be bused, they’ll be sent elsewhere, and they'll wander right back after the three-week Olympic and Paralympic events." Former Mayor Karen Bass accepted the Olympic flag during the closing ceremony in Paris two years ago, marking the handoff of hosting duties. This will be the first time LA has hosted the Games since 1984. According to the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority’s 2026 annual count, homelessness rose 3.4% in LA and 1.2% across the broader LA area, undoing two consecutive years of declines under Bass. But how does Raman plan to follow through on that promise? By the end of her first term, Raman has pledged to expand housing, shelter capacity and rental assistance to eliminate long-term encampments. Raman has previously called the city's "desensitization to homelessness" a "moral failing." Her plan calls for sending medical teams directly into encampments to provide mental health and addiction treatment and help with transitions into long-term housing or care within 90 days. Raman has also criticized Bass' Inside Safe program, which often places homeless people in costly hotels and motels. Instead, Raman wants to shift funding toward less expensive alternatives, like rental vouchers. SEATTLE MAYOR KATIE WILSON'S SOCIALIST AGENDA STALLS AMID HOMELESSNESS AND PUBLIC SAFETY CONCERNS Other parts of Raman’s proposal include sending unarmed crisis response teams rather than police officers to certain emergencies, auditing stalled housing projects and increasing oversight of homelessness spending. Despite Raman’s ambitious vision, Alle said he isn't convinced her plan will bring meaningful change and argued that city leadership has gone "from bad to worse." "It's not that much different than Mayor Karen Bass's plan," Alle said. Alle, who manages roughly 1 million square feet of commercial property across Los Angeles, said he sees the homelessness crisis firsthand and raised concerns about its impact on local businesses and workers. He warned that treating homeless people on the streets will only prolong the crisis, saying that many Angelenos avoid parts of the city that have been left untouched. "Pick up the individuals and take them to their facilities away from the parks, away from kids, away from seniors," he said. Alle said there must be more transparency over how the city has handled more than $1 billion in homelessness funding before allocating more taxpayer dollars. "She’s got a billion-dollar problem on her hands right now, and she knows," he said. FURIOUS RESIDENTS CONFRONT HOMELESS HOUSING LEADERS AS POPULAR BEACH COMMUNITY HITS BREAKING POINT Raman chaired the City Council's Housing and Homelessness Committee from 2023 until her removal this year amid her mayoral campaign. Alle said Raman will have to explain where the money went but acknowledged her push to investigate the spending. "To her credit, she wants to audit every single non-profit and every single agency that spent money, including the non-profits that are supported by the city with taxpayer funds for programs," he said. One of the biggest red flags in Raman’s plan is the proximity of supportive housing to families and children, according to Alle. He added that some facilities don't require residents to remain sober. "There is no commitment for anyone not to use drugs while they're there," he said. Pointing to her past opposition to restrictions on camping in public spaces and near schools, Alle argued Raman's approach isn’t "aggressive enough." "I don't see the solutions that have been put forth that could work being used and so I'm not optimistic," he said. Alle described LA as having a drug and mental health problem, not a homelessness problem. He said the city needs to stop making life on the streets more comfortable for those who refuse help. "Until those two issues are addressed, we're not gonna solve homelessness," he said. He urged Raman to find a more practical solution by moving outreach services off the streets and ending LA's sanctuary city status for good. "Of course I want her to succeed," he said. "If Nithya succeeds, we all succeed." Raman ousted Bass in the midterm elections and will take office in December as mayor of Los Angeles, a city of roughly 4 million residents. articles.title: SEN BERNIE SANDERS: No more excuses: Democrats must deliver
articles.summary: Election Day Democrats won 250-plus House seats and 56 Senate seats. Now the American people demand action on Medicare for All and a wealth tax.
articles.body: On Election Day, the American people, all across the country, sent a very powerful message to our country’s ruling class. In a loud and surprisingly unified voice, they said NO to Trump’s pathological lying, his contempt for the Constitution and the rule of law, his narcissism, his corruption and his disastrous policies. But they also said something more. At a time when 60% of our people are living paycheck to paycheck, when we have unprecedented income and wealth inequality, when we have the highest rate of childhood poverty of any industrialized nation, when millions of seniors are unable to retire with dignity, and when our younger generation may end up having a lower standard of living than their parents, working families voted for change, REAL change. Despite billions of dollars in ugly and dishonest TV ads, Americans made it clear. They want an end to status quo politics and status quo policies that prop up a rigged economy and a corrupt campaign finance system. And it wasn't just the election results. According to a recent AP poll, 80% of registered voters want either "complete and total upheaval" or "substantial change" in how this country is run, including 97% of Democrats, 90% of independents and 58% of Republicans. BERNIE SANDERS WARNS DEMOCRATS NOT TO SPEND ALL THEIR TIME INVESTIGATING TRUMP On Election Day, Democrats won a massive victory. When the new Congress convenes, Democrats will have more than 250 members in the House and at least 55 members in the Senate. Democrats now have the votes to pass legislation that will greatly improve the lives of millions of working families. And that’s exactly what they must do. No more empty rhetoric and poll-driven messaging. No more telling people, over and over again, how terrible Donald Trump and the Republicans are. No more excuses. The new Democratic majority must deliver for a long-neglected working class. Will Trump veto that legislation? Maybe, maybe not. If he signs the bills, the American people will benefit and be grateful. If he doesn’t, Republicans will pay a terrible political price. In my view, here is some of what the new Democratic Congress must focus on: HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY' HEALTH CARE: Our health care system is broken and wildly expensive. We spend twice as much per person as other major countries, yet more than 90 million Americans are uninsured or underinsured, over half a million go bankrupt each year because of medical debt and more than 60,000 die unnecessarily because they cannot afford care. Health care must be a human right, not a privilege. Democrats must pass Medicare for All, now supported by 66% of Americans. As a first step in a four-year transition, we must lower Medicare eligibility to 55, expand coverage to include dental, vision and hearing, and guarantee health care for every child from birth through age 19. INCOME AND WEALTH INEQUALITY: We have more income and wealth inequality in America today than at any time in our history. The top 1% now owns more wealth than the bottom 93%. Elon Musk alone owns more wealth than the bottom 53% of American households. Democrats must pass a 5% wealth tax on billionaires, supported by 61% of Americans. The new funds raised would provide working-class families of four with a $12,000 direct payment, build 7 million affordable housing units, make public colleges and universities tuition-free, establish free child care for 13 million children and improve public education. RAISE THE MINIMUM WAGE: While the rich get richer, 60% of Americans live paycheck to paycheck. The federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour is a starvation wage. We must raise it to at least $20 an hour and pass the PRO Act to make it easier for workers to organize unions. A job must lift people out of poverty, not keep them in it. At this extraordinary moment in our history, we must restore faith in democracy. One way we do that is by delivering tangible benefits for working families. PROTECT SENIORS: One-third of seniors are struggling economically, and more than 20% try to survive on less than $15,000 a year. Nearly half of older Americans have no retirement savings. Meanwhile, billionaires pay the same amount into Social Security as someone earning $184,600. THERE IS A WAY TO FIX SOCIAL SECURITY. AND THE SOLUTION MIGHT SURPRISE YOU That is absurd. We must apply the Social Security payroll tax to all income above $250,000, including capital gains and dividends. This would increase benefits by $2,400 a year, lift millions of seniors out of poverty and extend Social Security's solvency for generations, without raising taxes on the bottom 91% of Americans. We must also restore guaranteed pensions so workers can retire with dignity. AI AND ROBOTICS: Big Tech oligarchs are investing trillions in artificial intelligence and robotics with virtually no regulation. AI is the most transformative technology in the history of humanity. Left unchecked, it could destroy tens of millions of jobs, devastate children's mental health, eviscerate privacy, drive up electricity rates and strain water supplies. Uncontrolled superintelligence could even threaten humanity's existence. We cannot allow a handful of oligarchs to dictate our future. Democrats must enact a national moratorium on AI data centers, supported by 63% of Americans, pause advanced AI development and ban superintelligence. THE AI REVOLUTION COULD BECOME A NATIONAL SECURITY DISASTER IF WE AREN'T CAREFUL CLIMATE CHANGE: Rising temperatures, deadly heat waves, massive forest fires and extreme weather make it clear that we must act boldly. Democrats must create millions of good-paying jobs by moving our energy systems away from fossil fuels and toward energy efficiency and sustainable energy. MILITARY SPENDING: The wars in Vietnam, Iraq and now Iran were based on lies. We spend more on the military than the next six countries combined, yet the Pentagon repeatedly fails independent audits and cannot account for trillions in spending. Trump's illegal war in Iran is costing us hundreds of billions of dollars. We must end this disastrous war, cut off funding for the genocidal government in Israel and substantially reduce military spending. ICE AND IMMIGRATION: Since Trump took office, ICE agents have shot American citizens, broken down doors and sent 5-year-old children to detention centers. These actions are immoral, unconstitutional and economically counterproductive. Democrats must rescind the $75 billion Republicans gave Trump for his ICE domestic army. Instead of terrorizing communities, we need comprehensive immigration reform and a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT CAMPAIGN FINANCE REFORM: Elon Musk and his billionaire friends poured a record-breaking $2 billion into recent elections. articles.title: NYC woman allegedly struck by LGBTQ+ activist after questioning trans youth treatments: 'Never have answers'
articles.summary: LGBTQ+ activist Jay Walker allegedly elbowed a counter-protester outside Mount Sinai Hospital in New York City as she questioned his support for youth transgender procedures.
articles.body: A woman says she was assaulted by a prominent LGBTQ+ activist at a recent New York City protest as she was questioning his push for transgender medical procedures for children, according to video of the incident provided by the alleged victim. Christiane Torello was a counter-protester at the rally outside Mount Sinai Hospital in Manhattan on Nov. 5 when she was allegedly elbowed in the chest by Jay Walker, the president of Gays Against Guns who also served as a 2026 NYC Pride Grand Marshal. Walker was part of a group rallying against the hospital's decision in September to end transgender treatments for minors to resolve a Department of Justice investigation into youth gender transition procedures. "The hospital is no longer providing any type of gender-affirming care for minors, including surgeries, puberty blockers and hormones," Torello told Fox News Digital. "There’s always a group of individuals who go to these protests to show their discomfort and displeasure with the hospital stopping these procedures because they want the children to transition. I usually go there in opposition to them. I support the hospital’s decision to stop providing that care. I always go by myself and ask questions." MAJOR BLUE STATE HOSPITAL PULLS PLUG ON CONTROVERSIAL CHILD TRANSGENDER TREATMENTS AFTER DOJ INTERVENTION In the video she captured of the incident, Torello questioned Walker why he wanted to "have penises in the locker room" as he was yelling and walking away from her on a sidewalk. Walker then stopped, wound his elbow up and allegedly struck her in the chest before repeatedly shouting at her to "get away from me." She said demonstrators often attempt to obstruct her path and shove their signs in her face, but that this incident was more violent than most of the rallies she has been to. "I'm usually followed around the protest by two or three people. They block me and put signs in my face, which is fine because they’re allowed to do that. But this time, it became particularly violent," Torello said. "When I asked the organizer of the protest, Jay Walker, what size dongs he’d like in the girls’ locker room, he didn’t have an answer. They never have answers to those questions. They don’t like to talk about it," she continued. Torello said Walker was shouting slurs at her as he was walking away from the protest and she followed him to question him more about what he was saying. She then accused Walker of hitting her in the chest with his elbow, adding that she thinks he intended to strike her in the face but had "pretty bad aim." "As we were walking, he stopped in front of me, wound up his elbow and blasted me in the chest," she said. "He’s about 6'5" and I’m 5'5", so I’m pretty sure he intended to hit me in the face but had pretty bad aim and hit me in the chest." After the alleged assault, Torello continued following Walker down the street. UTAH STUDENT CITED AFTER PHYSICAL ALTERCATION WITH COLLEGE REPUBLICAN CAUGHT ON CAMERA The video shows both Torello and Walker yelling and cursing at one another as they were walking. Walker was heard calling her "psychotic," "scumbag," a "garbage person" and a "stalker," while she accused him of being a "woman abuser." At one point, he was allegedly seen lunging at Torello, to which she dared him to "do it again" and said she would post the video on social media. "I'm so glad I got it on camera," she shouted at Walker. Torello told Fox News Digital that she reported the incident to the New York City Police Department, but she is not confident any charges will be filed. "I want to press charges because I feel like New York doesn’t do anything when it comes to a lot of violence," she said. "But this is a different type of violence. I have a First Amendment right to be there and peacefully protest. I wasn’t hitting anybody. Do I ask questions that may be annoying or triggering? Sure. But that’s the extent of what I do. That doesn’t warrant me getting hit, elbowed or punched." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "This is actually the second time a man has put his hands on me at a protest," she continued. "The first happened about a month and a half ago. There were two NYPD detectives in front of that other protest who watched me get hit, and they didn’t even talk to me. I asked them if they could direct me somewhere, and they wouldn’t say one word to me. I had to figure it out on my own. I filed a report, and nothing happened to that man either." It is unclear if police plan to make any arrests in connection with the alleged assault. The NYPD and Walker's group, Gays Against Guns NY, did not respond to Fox News Digital's multiple requests for comment. "I just really hope this brings some awareness and puts pressure on the NYPD to do something, because they don’t do anything at all," Torello said.

articles.title: Schumer allies voice confidence, argue Van Hollen challenge about ending ‘filibuster’
articles.summary: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer’s (N.Y.) allies are predicting he will get more than 40 votes in his leadership contest against Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) while slamming the challenge as a “distraction.” That would be an overwhelming majority of the Senate Democratic caucus, which will have at least 55 members and possibly 56 if…
articles.body:
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer’s (N.Y.) allies are predicting he will get more than 40 votes in his leadership contest against Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) while slamming the challenge as a “distraction.”

That would be an overwhelming majority of the Senate Democratic caucus, which will have at least 55 members and possibly 56 if Democratic candidate Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska’s Senate race.

Schumer’s allies also are discussing the possibility of moving up the date of the Senate Democratic leadership election, which is now scheduled for the first week of December.

They say they want to take advantage of what they see as Schumer’s big lead in the early whip count and to unify the caucus as quickly as possible so that stories about internal Senate Democratic caucus squabbling don’t dominate news cycles over the next several weeks.

Changing the election date to sometime in November would require a vote of the Senate Democratic caucus.

One Schumer confidant said Van Hollen has no chance of winning and argued progressives are using his candidacy to exert leverage on Schumer to agree to a liberal wish list of priorities, such as “Medicare for All” and terminating the filibuster, which requires 60 votes to pass most legislation.

“It’s distracting,” said a Senate insider close to Schumer. “They’re going to try to get concessions out of the whole thing. Van Hollen doesn’t think he’s going to win. I think he’s trying to get some meat on the bone for the causes that the new members want.

“This is counterproductive,” the source said, adding that Van Hollen wasn’t actively calling colleagues to lock down votes for a potential leadership race until very recently.

Van Hollen, who announced his candidacy Thursday evening, acknowledged during a press conference at the What’s Next conference in Denver that he’s an “underdog” in the race.

“Let me be clear, I’m the underdog in this race. The majority leader has lots of powers of incumbency to try to make deals or agreements with people. That’s part of the problem with the process,” he said.

Van Hollen said he decided to run to close the “trust deficit” between voters and political leaders in Washington.

“I don’t think you can close the trust deficit by simply returning to the status quo or business as usual. That’s why I decided to run for the Senate majority leader position,” he said.

Van Hollen, as of Friday afternoon, had racked up four public commitments from progressive Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.).

He declined at the press conference to reveal his whip count of supporters.

Van Hollen’s allies think the push to move up the election date is a sign that Schumer is nervous that his 40-plus count of Senate Democratic supporters may be soft and could erode if calls for new leadership gather momentum from donors, activists and other rank-and-file Democrats.

“This is a classic ‘tell versus show’ situation. What he’s telling is that he has the votes and this isn’t competitive but what he’s showing by trying to change caucus rules is panic,” said a former Senate Democratic chief of staff.

Schumer has told Senate Democratic colleagues that he has locked up the votes he needs to be Democratic leader.

Another Senate Democratic insider said some Senate Democrats are upset that the party’s message on affordability may be derailed by media stories about Democratic infighting over leadership.

The source said members are “annoyed by” this because “we just came off a win” and could have had a narrative fully focused on Republicans trying to jam more funding for the Defense Department through Congress but instead there will be steady stream of news coverage about Democratic “infighting.”

Some Democratic senators had urged Van Hollen before his announcement not to risk dividing the caucus by announcing a long-shot leadership bid, said a person familiar with those internal conversations.

Van Hollen rejected that notion, arguing that the Democratic candidates who won on Election Day promised to change Washington and that the Democratic caucus “needs to be open to new ideas” and “a different way of governing.”

Van Hollen has a good chance of picking up public endorsements from Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), a leading progressive, and from Sens.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine), who made Medicare for All a core part of his campaign platform, and Juliana Stratton (D-Ill.), another progressive who has been outspoken about not backing Schumer.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) as of Friday hadn’t endorsed Van Hollen, but she told reporters in Denver that she’s “not voting for Sen. Schumer.”

Schumer’s supporters, however, are pointing to a growing list of public commitments from both centrists and progressive members of the Democratic caucus.

These include incoming Senate Democratic Whip Brian Schatz (Hawaii) and Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), Jack Reed (R.I.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Tammy Baldwin (Wis.), Angus King (I-Vt.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Kirsten Gillibrand (N.Y.) Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.) and Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (Ohio).

A Schumer ally said that other Democratic senators would either publicly endorse Schumer or vote for him by secret ballot, including Sens. Mark Warner (Va.), Tim Kaine (Va.), Cory Booker (N.J.), Andy Kim (N.J.), Ron Wyden (Ore.), Peter Welch (Vt.), Mazie Hirono (Hawaii), Angela Alsobrooks (Md.), Maggie Hassan (N.H.), Maria Cantwell (Wash.), Patty Murray (Wash.), Ben Ray Luján (N.M.), Jon Ossoff (Ga.), Raphael Warnock (Ga.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Adam Schiff (Calif.), John Hickenlooper (Colo.), and Michael Bennet (Colo.).

The source also said incoming Democratic Sens.-elect Roy Cooper (N.C.), Annie Andrews (S.C.), Mary Peltola (Alaska) and Josh Turek (Iowa) will vote for Schumer.

Another Schumer ally said that Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) and fellow Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D) are expected to also back Schumer.

Coons on Wednesday lauded Schumer’s leadership of the Senate Democrats’ political operation in this year’s election.

Blunt Rochester worked closely with Schumer to win back the Senate majority as vice chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee this cycle.

One Schumer ally noted that Schumer, as the presumptive favorite to be elected majority leader, is in a position to promise coveted committee assignments to incoming Democratic senators.

That might help sway the vote of uncommitted senators-elect, such as James Talarico of Texas and Chris Pappas of New Hampshire. It may also move Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.) to vote for Schumer.

While Hamilton pledged during the campaign not to vote for Schumer as leader and recently described him as “polarizing,” he might have a tough time justifying a vote for Van Hollen, who is clearly more progressive than Schumer and has endorsed Medicare for All and abolishing the Senate filibuster.

One of Hamilton’s trusted political advisors is Guy Cecil, who served as political director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee when Schumer chaired the Senate Democratic campaign arm.

articles.title: Senate Democrats prepare to flex new oversight powers against Musk
articles.summary: Democrats have spent the first half of the second Trump presidency openly questioning how Elon Musk has wielded influence over the federal government. Soon, they will have the chance to ask him directly. Fresh off a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, Senate Democrats are keen to use their new majority to investigate Musk and…
articles.body:
Democrats have spent the first half of the second Trump presidency openly questioning how Elon Musk has wielded influence over the federal government.

Soon, they will have the chance to ask him directly.

Fresh off a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, Senate Democrats are keen to use their new majority to investigate Musk and examine how intertwined his companies’ technology is with politics and global affairs.

Musk, the CEO of SpaceX and Tesla and the world’s wealthiest person, has been a long-sought target of Democratic oversight.

The billionaire entrepreneur became heavily involved in Republican politics over the last two years, helping President Trump win a second term and working as a special government employee where his Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) took a chainsaw to the federal workforce.

Musk funneled money and energy into protecting congressional Republicans; and to date, Republicans have protected him from facing questions in Congress.

Last year, Democrats on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee wanted to subpoena Musk to testify about DOGE and his role in the Trump administration, but Republicans blocked the effort .

Now in the majority and armed with subpoena authority, Democrats are likely to demand documents and testimony from Musk and others in his orbit about an array of topics, from his tenure at DOGE to contacts with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Among the most pressing concerns for Democrats — and some Republicans — is a slowdown in Starlink, a satellite-based broadband provider run by Musk’s SpaceX, and its military equivalent Starshield.

Amid Ukraine’s ongoing war with Russia, there have been multiple instances of Starshield slowing down and affecting Ukrainian military capabilities: one in October and another on Nov. 12 .

Musk has said only Trump can order such a slowdown, since Starshield is owned and operated by the U.S. government, but later reports alleged that Musk ordered it.

“See you in January,” Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) wrote in a post on social platform X last week, tagging Musk.

Musk “has Ukrainian blood on his hands” after he “altered a global conflict with the flick of a switch,” Gallego wrote.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), a key ally of Ukraine in Congress, confirmed this week that Democrats are “looking into contracts involving SpaceX and other corruption.”

Sen. Chris Coons (Del.), who is almost certain to be the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee next year, said he had a “list of questions for Musk when I subpoena him,” including about Starshield and why Putin called him a “real genius.”

“If Elon Musk has the power individually based on his whim or his politics or his sense of the strategic situation to switch off an absolutely vital strategic service to the defense services of Ukraine that we the American taxpayers are paying for, then we’ve got too much power accumulated in the hands of one man,” Coons said on CBS News last month .

Coons repeated the call to look into Musk’s involvement this past week.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.), the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, also called for investigations into Musk.

“The American people deserve answers about the loss of Ukraine’s Starlink and Starshield services, which put American personnel in Ukraine unnecessarily at risk and raise questions about whether the U.S. military should hold billions of dollars in contracts for a service they cannot control,” Shaheen, who is retiring, said in a statement.

Shaheen and retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis (N.C.) on Thursday issued a letter urging Congress to investigate the Starshield disruptions in Ukraine.

Neither senator will be in the next Congress though, when the Democratic-led investigations are likely to take place.

Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) said on MS NOW last month that he’s interested in multiple avenues on which to investigate Musk, including his DOGE work and other government contracts, but especially the Starlink debacle.

“It’s not just he’s a successful private sector individual,” Padilla said. “The role he played [as] unconfirmed unelected leader of this DOGE experiment, which had tremendous costs for the American people, not savings, the level of government contracts, the decisionmaking that he’s been a part of, the role he may or may not be playing in Ukraine and their reliability of Starlink as they’re trying to defend themselves against Russia who Donald Trump is clearly favoring more and more every single day.”

Musk has spent recent days defending his government contracts in anticipation of Democratic scrutiny.

“SpaceX contracts with the government are BOTH the best product AND the lowest price!” he wrote on X, which he owns.

“Happy to cancel any that the government doesn’t want. Just say the word!” Musk added.

Several Democrats in the House, including on relevant committees with oversight of Musk’s government ties, have also said they want to pursue investigations.

“I think there’s a lot of interest, not just from our committee, but from committees across the Congress to speak to Mr. Musk,” Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the likely chair of the House Oversight Committee, said on CNN’s “State of the Union” just after the election.

“Elon Musk waved a chainsaw on stage and laughed while he fired public servants and gutted the services Americans rely on. … He must answer for it under oath,” Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) wrote on X .

It’s possible that some Republicans could join investigations related to the Starshield lapse.

Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, expressed some concern over Musk’s dominance of space.

Cramer told reporters later in October after receiving a classified update about the Starshield disruption that he’s not totally comfortable that Musk “has as much power as he does as one individual and one company over America’s ability to protect the domain of space, which is a warfighting domain.”

But most of the lawmakers who have criticized Musk are retiring or lost their reelection bids.

For instance, four Republican senators joined with Democrats in October to press the Trump administration for information about whether Pentagon officials ordered restrictions on Ukraine’s access to the satellite-based Starshield network.

But among those Republicans — Sens. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), John Cornyn (Texas), Susan Collins (Maine) and Tillis — only Murkowski will return.
