articles.title: Trump keeps signaling an end to Iran war, but expert warns a crucial piece of his strategy is missing
articles.summary: President Donald Trump declared on Truth Social the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Iran, one day after proclaiming victory at Arlington.
articles.body: President Donald Trump declared Thursday that the United States no longer needs a deal with Iran, abruptly shifting his diplomatic message just three days after expressing optimism about negotiations and directing Vice President JD Vance to focus on domestic issues instead. "We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!" Trump's latest declaration came just one day after he proclaimed victory over Iran during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery, while acknowledging that the conflict had not yet formally ended. "We won," Trump said Wednesday. "It’s just a question of when we end it. I want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93 percent victory." TRUMP DEFENDS IRAN WAR DURING VETERANS DAY ADDRESS, SAYS HE IS MAKING THE WORLD 'SAFER' The president also thanked veterans "working to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of state terrorism, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never have a nuclear weapon." An administration official defended Trump's strategy, arguing that the United States has substantial leverage over Iran through its naval blockade and continued military pressure, even as questions remain about how the conflict will end. "The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. The President has been clear that the greatest naval blockade in history, Operation Economic Outcast, and the new Operation Iron Gate will continue with full effect," a U.S. official told Fox News Digital. "President Trump holds all the cards, will do what is best for the United States, and will make sure that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon," the official added. Trump's latest words follow months of predictions that an agreement could be reached soon, including comments earlier this week that Tehran "would love to make a deal." Trump's declaration raises questions about the future of U.S.-Iran negotiations, including whether diplomatic efforts will continue through other administration officials as Washington maintains its military and economic pressure on Tehran. AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR? Trump has suggested on at least a dozen occasions since February that Iran wanted to negotiate or that an agreement could be reached soon, according to a preliminary review of his public remarks. Ludovic Hood, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, said the administration's combination of economic coercion, military force and regional partnerships is sensible, but warned that a crucial diplomatic component remains underdeveloped. "What’s lacking is disciplined diplomacy to complement the economic squeeze and possible airstrikes," Hood told Fox News Digital. "Our Gulf partners are singing from different hymn sheets and we need to draw European partners in more meaningfully." Trump's optimistic assessments began before U.S. military operations against Iran commenced. On Feb. 13, he suggested Tehran could avoid an attack by accepting Washington's terms. After military operations began, he increasingly emphasized Iran's weakened capabilities and the prospect of ending the conflict. IRANIAN NEGOTIATORS KICKED OUT OF US AS TALKS STALL, TRUMP LAYS OUT 'POSSIBLE' TIMELINE FOR MORE STRIKES On March 20, Trump said the United States was "getting very close" to achieving its military objectives. The administration agreed to a ceasefire in April and continued pursuing a diplomatic settlement, but subsequent military actions and disagreements over Iran's nuclear program and regional shipping have left the broader conflict unresolved. Trump continued expressing confidence that Iran wanted an agreement, including in May, when he suggested Tehran was eager to negotiate because of the damage inflicted on its military. During an unscheduled appearance in the White House briefing room Monday, Trump said, "Iran, militarily, is effectively over," while warning that U.S. forces remained "locked and loaded" should circumstances change. Hood said Trump's seemingly contradictory messages could be part of a deliberate negotiating strategy. "The administration is pursuing a sensible hybrid strategy of economic coercion, selective use of force, and reliance on capable regional allies," Hood said. TRUMP SAYS IRAN IS 'NEGOTIATING ON FUMES,' BELIEVES REGIME THOUGHT THEY COULD OUTWAIT HIM "Trump’s messaging seems designed to both signal his preference for a diplomatic solution while preserving the option of force," he added. Hood defended the president's willingness to maintain military pressure. "Bluster, bluffing and brinkmanship are inherent in the public dimension of negotiations like this; Trump does it, Rubio does it, and senior figures in Tehran do it," he said. "Strategic patience is essential in this standoff, which has essentially been 40 years in the making." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But Hood also suggested that securing meaningful nuclear concessions or a more cooperative government in Tehran would require coordination with regional partners.

articles.title: Inside the House GOP strategy to capitalize on Democrats' warring factions in the new Congress
articles.summary: Tom Emmer says House Republicans will use committee hearings and floor votes to hold Democrats accountable as the GOP shifts to minority status.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: House Republicans are heading into the next Congress ready to brawl. Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., who is set to go from the No. 3 most powerful House Republican to No. 2 next year, told Fox News Digital that the GOP will hold the new Democrat majority "accountable" for their far-left faction's ideas over the next two years, even if they cannot control what bills get a vote. Emmer, who has served as House majority whip for the past four years, was elected Tuesday to serve as minority whip alongside incoming House Minority Leader Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. The Speaker of the House position turns over to Democrats, and will likely be won by current minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. And despite Jeffries poised to take control of what legislation gets to the House floor, Emmer signaled House Republicans would find ways to push their agenda as well. JIM JORDAN BECOMES NEW HOUSE GOP LEADER AFTER CLOSED-DOOR VOTE, DEFEATING STEVE SCALISE "What's their answer to dealing with costs and wages? We're going to investigate Trump," Emmer said in reference to Democrats. "That's not going to solve the problems that they created. So that's going to be the job of the whip, is to make sure that we have a coordinated process — committee hearings, floor votes — to expose and define exactly who these people really are." PROGRESSIVE GROUP'S 182-PAGE BLUEPRINT MAPS OUT POTENTIAL DEM INVESTIGATIONS INTO TRUMP, CORPORATE ALLIES Emmer, in his first print interview since winning the House minority whip job, would not go into detail about how Republicans would utilize floor votes, however. "There's a toolbox with a bunch of different tools, and you're going to have to build that strategy as you go from week to week," he said. The Minnesota Republican also signaled there would be little appetite for bipartisanship over the next two years, a sentiment he suggested would come from the other side of the aisle. "Well look, they're not going to work with us, that's pretty clear, and I don't even know if they're going to be able to work with each other," Emmer said. HAKEEM JEFFRIES FACES PROGRESSIVE HOLDOUTS BUT NO RIVAL AS HOUSE SPEAKER RACE TAKES SHAPE He repeated a short time later, "I see nowhere where they're going to work with Republicans. And Republicans who think they are should think again, because they will tell you nice things, and then they will just go do what they do." Meanwhile other House Republicans are already coming up with ideas on how to put Democrats on the spot on the House floor in the new Congress. "We'll file amendments," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "And I think that'll be where having good debaters and communicators would be important." Holding amendment votes is commonplace before large pieces of legislation like the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which Congress has enacted annually for decades to update and reauthorize critical national security policies. Rep. Nick LaLota, R-N.Y., suggested an emphasis on a parliamentary procedure called the "motion to recommit," which allows the minority party to get a vote on altering or even killing a bill in its tracks. "I expect we'll use that smartly," LaLota said. "But as well, a Speaker Hakeem Jeffries will be wise to work these problems backwards, to know that anything he puts on the floor that he wants to become law or budget needs President Trump's signature and probably 60 votes in the Senate." Rep. Mark Harris, R-N.C., said "there's been a lot of conversation about going on offense." "We want to make sure that they know when they come to the floor, they're gonna dread it, I hope," Harris said. DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY But there's another mechanism for forcing a House vote that's been used more and more often in recent years — often by their fellow Republicans. Privileged resolutions allow lawmakers on either side to get a vote on a given bill within two days of its introduction. It generally begins with a procedural vote on whether to "table" the bill or refer it to committee in order to stop it, before a vote on the measure itself. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., most recently invoked it to force the House to consider impeaching Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. But that was defeated when the rest of the House GOP banded together to refer the bill to committee. The GOP lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital, however, signaled little appetite for using it. "I think either party would be wise to build consensus around things that help actually deliver for the American people," LaLota said. "The privileged resolutions have been abused in my time here, and there's a better way to do business." And Emmer said his main goal for the next two years would be winning back the House majority in 2028 — which he insisted was a realistic goal. He said at least 38 seats flipped by Democrats would be "ready to return to Republican hands," and could see some old faces return. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Asked whether he wanted to see some of those losing GOP incumbents run for their seats again, Emmer said, "I absolutely hope so, I've talked to several already."

articles.title: The 2028 presidential race is already full of surprises, prediction markets say
articles.summary: The 2028 presidential market report shows Jon Ossoff leading Democrats at 26% despite a third of his party never having heard of him.
articles.body: The 2028 presidential election seems far away. Or is it already here? The midterm ballots are barely counted, and a long list of would-be candidates is already elbowing for a lane in a campaign that, by Election Day, will feel like it started during the Truman administration. Outside the Super Bowl, few things are as popular on prediction markets as a presidential race. Two years before anyone casts a ballot, Kalshi's 2028 markets have already drawn nearly half a billion dollars in trading. While prediction markets have an excellent long-term record of accuracy, this far from an election, you can't expect surgical precision. STU BURGUIERE: PUT YOUR MONEY WHERE YOUR MOUTH IS: PREDICTION MARKETS WON THE MIDTERMS What the markets can show us is who's trading like a blue chip, who's stuck in the middle, and whose campaign feels like a penny stock that needs a miracle rally to be competitive. So let's look ahead with a way-too-early presidential market report, starting at the top. The blue chips What if I told you the Democratic front-runner for 2028 is a man a third of Democrats have never heard of? That's what a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found when it comes to Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, and plenty of other Americans are drawing a blank too. Still, a Democrat who wins Georgia by 18 points, in a state President Trump carried in 2024, doesn’t stay anonymous for long. Kalshi gives him a 26% chance of winning the Democratic nomination, the best in the field. Not bad for a guy much of his own party couldn't pick out of a lineup. NEW POLL COMPLICATES VANCE’S STATUS AS TRUMP’S LIKELY 2028 HEIR APPARENT On the Republican side, Vice President J.D. Vance leads the pack, with a 33% chance of winning the nomination but only a 12% chance of winning the presidency. That gap fits what election analyst Nate Silver calls the VP curse. Vice presidents whose bosses are underwater in the polls tend to win their party’s nomination, then lose in November. Then again, Vance has been underestimated before, and he seems to be at his best in high-leverage situations. Both men have also hinted they might not run at all. Coming from politicians, that promise has roughly the credibility of a vow of celibacy from Jensen Huang. The mid-caps California Gov. Gavin Newsom looked like a blue chip a year ago. His chance of winning the Democratic nomination has since cratered from 37% to about 12%. He leaves office in January, which frees him up for a full-time campaign and gives even more airtime to a man who has never been accused of camera shyness. Whether voters want that is another question. AOC TAPS POWER PLAYER WHO HELPED BERNIE SANDERS DEFY THE ODDS AS MAJOR 2028 DECISION LOOMS Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez sits around 13% to win the Democratic nomination. The bigger question is which race she's running in. Traders actually think she's more likely to run for the Senate than for president. Either way, somebody is going to claim the democratic socialist lane. If it's not her, maybe Bernie Sanders takes a third crack at it. He'll only be 87. Like Ocasio-Cortez, Secretary of State Marco Rubio faces a which-job question. He's at 18% to win the Republican nomination, and the market sees him as just as likely to be the running mate as the nominee. VANCE, CRUZ AND DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS BATTLE OVER PARTY'S FUTURE BEGINS Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who ran in 2024 and also leaves office in January, has been the biggest riser in the Republican market since the midterms. He was under 5% to win the nomination before the votes were counted and is now at 17%, nipping at Rubio's heels. The penny stocks Then come the penny stocks. On the Democratic side, that's a crowd in the single digits for the nomination: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. Former Vice President Kamala Harris lands here too, a somewhat embarrassing showing for the woman at the top of the ticket two years ago. If you're shopping the bargain bin, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore at 2.2% and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer at 0.7% might be in your wheelhouse. (In dead last, at 0.0%: Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz.) Josh Hawley could be value plays. And somewhere in that mix is President Donald Trump, who I wouldn't put past publicly flirting with a constitutionally prohibited third run just to annoy the media. The long-term outlook Many of these names won’t make it to the first primary. Today’s penny stock could be next summer’s blue chip. That’s the fun of watching these markets this early: prices will move with every speech, stumble and suspiciously timed book tour between now and then. articles.title: GOP newcomer who toppled Cory Mills sets sights on fraud, inflation as he heads to Capitol Hill
articles.summary: Rep.-elect Ryan Elijah, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital he wants to crack down on fraud and congressional insider trading.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: Florida Republican congressman-elect Ryan Elijah told Fox News Digital that he is heading to Washington with an "appetite" to crack down on fraud, protect consumers and tackle inflation, while calling for bipartisan cooperation in the incoming Congress. Elijah, a former Central Florida sports broadcaster, made his remarks amid heightened scrutiny of fraud involving taxpayer-funded federal programs across the country. "I'm going to lean into consumer protection — that's something I fought for my whole life — and lean into fraud," Elijah told Fox News Digital. "There is so much more Washington could do against fraud. I hope there is a bipartisan appetite on both sides to not only protect consumers but also target some of this fraud that is wasting so much of our tax dollars." The incoming Republican, who beat embattled Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., in the Republican primary in August, expressed optimism that lawmakers from both parties could find common ground on addressing fraud and rising costs, arguing that voters sent a clear message during Tuesday's midterm elections. Elijah said voters "made it loud and clear to both parties" that they "want change, they want inflation to come down, and they want life to become a little easier. So I think both parties need to look at that." Elijah also emphasized that members of Congress represent "100% of the people in their district, not just 50%," arguing that bipartisan solutions are necessary to restore public trust and accountability in Washington. FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM' Beyond fighting fraud, Elijah pledged to restore a spirit of public service to Congress, criticizing lawmakers who use their positions to enrich themselves. "What you do see is the people that enhance themselves, and people don't want to see that. None of that should be taking place," Elijah said while discussing congressional insider trading. "Members of Congress should not sit on a committee and be able to trade stocks, and that is something that I would support if it moves forward in the next Congress," he continued. "We all have to be on the same playing field, the person back home and the person on Capitol Hill." Elijah outlined his preferred committee assignments, telling Fox News Digital that he would like to serve on the House Energy and Commerce Committee or the House Financial Services Committee, where he could focus on consumer protection and financial oversight. He also expressed interest in serving on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, describing it as "a great way to bring projects back to my district." Elijah said his district has "so much growth ahead of us," arguing that a seat on the committee could help address its infrastructure needs. The incoming lawmaker addressed the challenges facing Republicans after losing control of Congress in the midterm elections, urging his party to remain united. Elijah said Republicans must "hold the line" on the "progress we've made so far" while working to advance their priorities in a divided Washington. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Elijah is expected to be sworn into the 120th Congress in January.

articles.title: Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting at APEC: What to expect
articles.summary: A nuclear treaty and the US’s war on Iran are among priority topics for China, Russia and US leaders.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump, China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen, the White House has confirmed .

On Friday, Washington also confirmed Trump’s attendance at the summit, which will take place from November 18-19.

Talks will focus on nuclear proliferation, the White House said. But they come amid significant global turbulence: Russia’s war in Ukraine, the US-Israeli war on Iran and ongoing trade tensions between Washington and Beijing.

“I think what we’ll see is some pretty impressive photo-ops with a lot of really bombastic rhetoric from Trump,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at the UK’s Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera. However, he added, the three “collectively or unilaterally, are not able to bring about an end to the conflict in Iran or Ukraine”.

So what does each side want and what will be the likely outcome?

Each leader has his own priorities, but there are some issues all will want to discuss.

A top issue for Russia and the US is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which lapsed in February. The treaty was first signed in 2010 and caps US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.

Russia currently possesses the largest number of warheads, followed by the US and then China, which is rapidly building up its own arsenal.

Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty after it expired, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing.

China is understood, however, to be reluctant to join an agreement it was not involved in forming.

A senior Trump administration official told Reuters this topic will start the conversation but that “we do not expect to get any kind of agreement”.

Officials also say the world leaders will discuss the Iran war , which the US and Israel launched on February 28. While full-scale strikes have, for now, ceased, the conflict remains in a deadlock .

After more than 100 days, the critical Strait of Hormuz remains closed, and oil and gas prices are still volatile as ships in the strait continue to face Iranian strikes and seamines. One-third of China’s crude oil supply transited the strait before the war. The conflict is also hampering demand for Chinese exports.

Russia, meanwhile, has profited from rising energy prices and recent sanctions relief from Washington amid supply crunches – particularly of diesel.

Trade wars and the race to control microchips used to power artificial intelligence are straining relations between Beijing and Washington.

Trump hit China with a 145 percent tax hike last year, while Beijing retaliated by imposing 125 percent levies on US imports. Tensions mounted further over China’s restrictions on exports of rare earth minerals needed to manufacture advanced chips and other technology.

The two countries have since reduced tariffs and struck several deals following Trump and Xi’s meetings in South Korea and Washington However, the recent scandal at chip firm Nvidia has prompted the US to allege that China was spying on CEO Jensen Huang. Beijing denies this.

It is very unlikely. A Trump administration official told reporters the US president will not bring up Russia’s war on Ukraine, although Kremlin officials previously suggested the conflict could be discussed.

China, an ally of Moscow’s, has said the Ukraine war is a European issue.

US officials also note that Washington is pursuing peace talks, with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visiting both Ukraine and Russia this week. “China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” an official told reporters.

President Trump has accused Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of “not wanting” to end the war, while Kyiv has reiterated allegations that the US has restricted its Starlink satellite connection that allows it to operate attack drones. Trump has also blamed Ukraine for soaring diesel prices because of its strikes on Russian oil facilities.

At the same time, Trump has feted Putin, agreed to allow Russian diesel into global and US markets, and lifted oil sanctions on Moscow.

What does each side want from this meeting?

For President Putin, the meeting could provide a positive photo opportunity and a platform to project power while sidelining the Ukraine conflict, analysts say.

It will give him a “first among equals” position that he can display at home to show that he can influence Europe’s security architecture following the Ukraine war, Alexander Bratersky, a Moscow-based journalist and political analyst, told Al Jazeera.

Beijing has already been pushing for a resolution to the US war on Iran, which has impacted its own energy supplies.

China will also want to avoid being pulled into a nuclear treaty it had no part in establishing.

Last month, China’s Foreign Ministry said it would be “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage”.

Trump’s priority is to include both China and Russia in a new nuclear proliferation treaty, according to administration officials. “The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, told reporters.

The president could also use the meeting to project his administration’s diplomatic influence, as Iran refuses to capitulate to US demands for ending the war and hand Washington a win.

Trump has also sought closer ties with Xi, Putin and North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, all seen as “strongmen”, and is likely to be perceived as influential in such circles, analysts say.

“I think it will be more performative – Donald Trump playing global statesman rather than peacemaker,” said Mabon.

Trump’s Republican Party’s crushing defeat in midterm elections last week could undermine his leverage, experts note, as a new Democrat-led Congress is likely to support Ukraine more staunchly.

Pyotr Tolstoy, chairman of the Russian parliament’s foreign affairs committee said it could lead to a “new Yalta”.

The 1945 conference in Yalta, in the then Soviet Union, saw USSR President Joseph Stalin, the US’s Franklin D Roosevelt, and the United Kingdom’s Winston Churchill divide Germany and establish the United Nations in what was seen as the template for a new world order.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, called the trilateral meeting now taking place between the leaders of the US, China and Russia as “extremely significant” but pointed out that any agreements reached at the meeting cannot be imposed on other nations.

articles.title: One industry surged DC lobbying 337% under Trump — here’s what’s driving the push
articles.summary: Lobbying spending on tariff-related filings surged 337% in 2026, Advancing American Freedom found, as businesses scramble to navigate trade shifts.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump has made tariffs a centerpiece of his trade agenda, and businesses are spending more on D.C. bureaucrats to help navigate those rules. Rachel Greszler, who authored a new report from Advancing American Freedom (AAF), said companies are paying lobbyists to seek exemptions from tariffs instead of using that money to grow their businesses, hire workers or raise wages. A new report from former Vice President Mike Pence's group found that lobbying disclosures mention tariffs rising 239% in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2024. The total spending reported on those filings jumped 337%, though it may include lobbying on issues beyond tariffs. A MUST-WIN MIDTERM STATE IS THE REAL LOSER OF TRUMP'S CANADA TRADE WAR "Affordability is top of mind for many Americans," Greszler told Fox News Digital, arguing that changing tariffs are raising costs, threatening jobs and squeezing paychecks. Businesses are responding by stepping up their lobbying efforts. Fourteen organizations spent more than $1 million on lobbying in the third quarter, up from two in the same quarter of 2024. Another 105 spent more than $100,000, compared with 26 two years earlier. Tariffs may also be affecting prices consumers pay. TRUMP BET TARIFFS WOULD BRING BACK AMERICAN FACTORY JOBS. NEW REPORT SAYS IT DIDN'T WORK FLOURISH NY FED TARIFFS CHART: 30552508 Federal Reserve Bank of New York researchers estimated they added 2.9 percentage points to prices across the consumer goods they studied, including imported and U.S.-made products. Greszler warned that small businesses unable to afford lobbyists to seek tariff exclusions could be forced to scale back or close. Trump has defended tariffs as a central part of his trade agenda, arguing they will strengthen U.S. manufacturing and bring jobs and investment back to the country. The White House has also said foreign exporters will ultimately bear the cost. FLOURISH TARIFF REVENUES CHART: 30871804 A separate analysis from Advancing American Freedom estimated tariffs resulted in about 75,000 fewer manufacturing jobs in their first year and up to 1 million fewer jobs nationwide than would have been expected under pre-tariff trends. The group said manufacturing was among the hardest-hit sectors, despite being a central target of the administration’s effort to bring factory work back. The group also said U.S. trade with Canada fell by $50 billion, or 6.5%, before the latest round of Section 338 tariffs took effect. During that period, imports from other countries rose instead of U.S. manufacturing expanding. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As the administration continues to reshape trade policy, businesses will have to decide whether to keep spending on lobbyists and tariff planning or delay investments, hiring and expansion until the rules become clearer.

articles.title: Murderers face justice decades later. Why are child-rapists protected from older charges?
articles.summary: Federal legislation is needed to close the loopholes and harmonize the hodgepodge of laws against child sex abuse that currently exist in the United States.
articles.body:
Legally, there is a strange disconnect between how this country treats the crime of murder and how it treats the crime of sexually abusing a child. In too many jurisdictions, accused child-abusers are granted legal protections and advantages that people who have been accused of murder do not have access to.

Yet, in numerous surveys, most adults rank the crime of rape as roughly equivalent to that of murder.

The crime of raping a child stands at the very summit of most people’s ideas of criminality at its most horrific. Legal minds and policymakers from across the political spectrum agree on this. In the wake of the controversial Supreme Court decision in 2008’s Kennedy vs. Louisiana , presidential candidate Barack Obama found himself agreeing with Justice Samuel Alito’s dissent, in which he wrote, “In the eyes of ordinary Americans, the very worst child-rapists … are the epitome of moral depravity. ”

Yet in many parts of the U.S., those who rape children are protected by statutes of limitations. Unlike murderers, they cannot be made to stand trial for their crimes after a certain number of years has passed. In more than half of the U.S., that limit is pegged to the age of the victim. In other words, once victims pass that age, ranging anywhere from 24 to 55, they lose the right to bring charges against their attackers. In many cases, they even expose themselves to slander charges by going public with their claims after the lapse of many years.

If someone is murdered, a corpse is usually enough to trigger a criminal investigation. But when children are sexually abused, they need to file convincing reports with the proper authorities for anything to happen. Studies have shown that more than half of the victims of child sexual abuse wait until they are past the age of 50 before they come forward. It is common for abusers to swear the children to secrecy and threaten them with further consequences in the event of disclosure. The shame and trauma of the attack are usually enough on their own to ensure silence for years to come.

In my own case, after being raped by my violin professor at the Curtis Institute of Music in Philadelphia when I was 14, I made all of the usual mistakes. For months, I closed up, kept to myself and did nothing. Then I asked the dean to give me a new teacher. He scoffed at the idea and dragged his feet on taking action. After another painful year, I attempted suicide and then left Curtis. Decades passed before I went public with my story, in a cover feature in The Philadelphia Inquirer in 2019 .

Unfortunately, even though Pennsylvania passed a new law that year setting the higher cutoff age of 55 for childhood victims of sexual abuse to file charges, this applied only to new cases . It did nothing for people like me or other past victims of abuse. Under the applicable laws at the time, I had two years from the time of the attack in 1986 to file charges. The deadline expired when I was 16, emotionally and financially broken. It’s ridiculous to imagine that I could have lawyered up and done anything concrete to stop my attacker at that time.

Child rapists know this. They go after the most vulnerable kids, and they understand exactly how to game the laws that are intended to deter them. The institutions that shelter these people have also shown a keen awareness of just how much, or how little, is required of them to fulfill their obligations under the law.

And that is why federal legislation is needed to close the loopholes and harmonize the hodgepodge of laws against sexual abuse of children abuse that currently exist in the U.S.

There is no divergence of public opinion on whether the sexual abuse of children is good or bad. There is a rock-solid consensus across the political spectrum that it should be stamped out as much as possible. Childhood sex abuse ruins lives. It is more pernicious than simple murder. There are certain circumstances in which killing someone is fully defensible, ethically and under the law, but no one ever raped a child in self-defense.

The only force standing in the way of justice for victims is a narrow set of vested institutional interests seeking to limit their financial exposure to potential claims. That is not a good enough reason to protect child-rapists. American voters do not want their elected representatives to protect criminals. Congress needs to take action and strip them of their protections once and for all.

Lara St. John is a violinist and filmmaker. Her documentary, “Dear Lara,” on sexual abuse at music schools will be screened at the Alexandria Film Festival on Nov. 15.

articles.title: GOP midterm bloodbath exposes cracks in Vance's 2028 White House ambitions
articles.summary: Rep. Randy Fine compared JD Vance's post-midterm remarks on the Iran war to 1932 Germany, vowing he will not support a 2028 presidential bid.
articles.body: Vice President JD Vance has long been viewed as President Donald Trump's heir apparent, but a string of developments following Republicans' bruising midterm losses is raising new questions about his potential path to the White House in 2028. Vance is facing criticism from some Republicans over his explanation for the party's election defeats, particularly his decision to blame the Iran war. Meanwhile, other prominent Republicans are beginning to draw support for potential 2028 bids, complicating the political picture for the vice president. The political debate follows a devastating election for Republicans, who lost their majorities in both chambers of Congress beginning next year, with at least 30 GOP House members losing their races. The losses have prompted competing explanations from within the party over what went wrong and what Republicans should do differently. Some of Vance's allies have reportedly urged him to consider sitting out the 2028 race following the midterm losses, The Wall Street Journal reported Nov. 7. However, others close to the vice president still expect him to run, The Washington Post reported Friday, underscoring the uncertainty surrounding his political future. TRUMP SAYS HE DOESN’T DISAGREE WITH VANCE THAT IRAN WAR FUELED GOP LOSSES A Vance ally pushed back on suggestions that the midterm losses have diminished his 2028 prospects, saying the vice president will decide whether to run on his own timeline. The ally also argued that Vance would be better served by winning a competitive Republican primary than being handed the nomination, expressing confidence in his ability to prevail if he runs. In a Nov. 4 post on X, Vance identified several concerns among voters who abandoned Republicans, including inflation, America First priorities and the U.S. relationship with Israel, but singled out the Iran war as the main reason for the party's defeats. "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote, adding that Republicans needed to acknowledge the political cost of the conflict as they consider where to go next. The post drew sharp criticism from Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., who told Fox' LiveNOW in a Nov. 8 interview that he would not support Vance in a potential 2028 presidential primary. PENCE DELIVERS SCATHING REBUKE OF VANCE'S IRAN WAR ASSESSMENT, BLAMES TRUMP POLICIES FOR GOP LOSSES "I definitively will not be supporting the vice president in that nominating contest," Fine said, comparing Vance's remarks to rhetoric from "1932 Germany." Fine, who is Jewish, accused Vance of blaming Jewish people for the Republican losses, pointing to his criticism of the war and the pollster's finding that some voters wanted a change in America's relationship with Israel. Vance did not explicitly blame Jewish people in his post, and his office previously declined to respond to Fine's characterization. VANCE COURTING DISGRUNTLED TRUMP VOTERS TO FORM ‘NEW RIGHT’ ALLIANCE AFTER REPUBLICAN BLOODBATH, SOURCES SAY Some Republicans are already expressing support for possible alternatives to Vance. Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital after the midterms that he was "all in" for Secretary of State Marco Rubio, describing him as a potential unifying figure for Republicans following their election losses. Rubio is among several prominent Republicans whose names have surfaced as possible 2028 presidential contenders, along with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas. Former Vice President Mike Pence also disputed Vance's explanation for Republicans' midterm losses, arguing in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview Thursday that voters had grown frustrated not because Trump launched the Iran war, but because his administration failed to finish it. "There's no question that the war in Iran became a frustration for millions of Americans, but it wasn't because President Trump started the war or took on Iran. It's because we stopped short and didn't finish it," Pence said. "As Americans saw the politics of appeasement that the administration embraced, one negotiation after another, I think people became ... frustrated with the lack of progress, frustrated with the price of fuel at the pump." Trump, meanwhile, has publicly defended Vance's assessment of the midterms, rejecting suggestions that the remarks damaged their relationship. "No, not at all," Trump told reporters Sunday when asked whether Vance's comments had strained their relationship, according to The Hill. But the president also stood by his decision to launch the war, arguing that he would make the same choice again despite the political fallout. Donald Trump Jr. also backed Vance's assessment, writing "Every word of this is [100 emojis]" in response to his Nov. 4 post on X. On Thursday, Trump directed Vance to focus his attention on alleged corruption and crime in Democratic-led cities and states rather than pursuing negotiations with Iran, declaring that the United States no longer needed a deal with Tehran. Vance had played a central role in diplomatic efforts involving Iran, including negotiations over a short-lived truce earlier this year. "The Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters," Trump wrote in the post. "Billions of Dollars is being stolen each and every month. Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large scale criminal activity. CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership’s blood!" "We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!" the president continued. VANCE ‘PRIVATELY’ BLASTS NETANYAHU AS IRAN WAR DIVIDES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AND 2028 AMBITIONS LOOM Trump has previously signaled support for Vance as his potential successor, telling donors during an Oval Office meeting over the summer that Republicans needed to elect the vice president in 2028, Fox News Digital reported at the time. But Trump has stopped short of publicly endorsing Vance, and the president has continued to leave open the possibility of other Republicans entering the race. When asked on Nov. 4 whether he had talked about a prospective 2028 White House run with Vance, Trump replied that the two discuss "a lot of things," Axios reported. Trump added: "Maybe he [Vance] won't run. I don't know who's going to run." Still, Vance told Mark Halperin in an October interview that he believes Trump would back him if he jumps into the presidential race, ABC 7 reported. "I really have not made up my mind about what to do in 2028. I just haven't focused on it. We, you, and I have talked about that. Look, I think if I run, the president will endorse me," Vance said during the interview. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital's Ashley DiMella and Fox News' Paul Steinhauser contributed to this story.

articles.title: Peltola holds nearly 4-point lead on Sullivan in latest ballot drop
articles.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola has again expanded her lead in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race with more votes counted, now ahead of Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) by nearly 4 points, or more than 10,000 votes, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Peltola netted nearly 2,000 votes from the latest batch of votes added. The Alaska Democrat now…
articles.body:
Democrat Mary Peltola has again expanded her lead in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race with more votes counted, now ahead of Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) by nearly 4 points, or more than 10,000 votes, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Peltola netted nearly 2,000 votes from the latest batch of votes added.

The Alaska Democrat now has 49.8 percent of the vote, just shy of a majority, which she would need to avoid an instant runoff using ranked choice voting. With 91 percent of votes counted, the former congresswoman now has a real chance to surpass 50 percent.

In a statement shared to the social platform X on Friday, Peltola’s campaign again declared victory after the new vote drop.

“There is no mathematical path for Sullivan to win this race,” the statement reads. “When the remaining votes are counted, Mary will decisively be elected as Alaska’s next United States Senator.”

Sullivan’s campaign account has not posted since Nov. 4. DDHQ has not called this race as of Saturday morning.

Votes from Alaska will continue to trickle in throughout next week, but all must be counted and reported by Nov. 18. If Peltola still does not reach a majority of the vote by then, the ranked choice voting tabulation would take place.

Peltola avoiding ranked choice is potentially significant in another way. The Trump administration previously sued to block the certification of the Senate race if Sullivan lost, because of the presence of another candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot.

The Justice Department argued that if Peltola won by less than the amount of votes the non-incumbent Sullivan received, then they could argue the candidate’s presence confused voters. That lawsuit was ultimately dismissed , and if Peltola’s current lead holds, the administration would not be able to make the same case.

A win for Peltola would be significant for Democrats, giving the party a 56th Senate seat after its already strong midterm performance. It would also make it less likely that the GOP would be able to win back the chamber in 2028, even if they win the presidency.

Elsewhere in Alaska, DDHQ projected that Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the gubernatorial contest , a pickup for Democrats. The U.S. House race is still uncalled , but Rep. Nick Begich III (R) leads. DDHQ projected that contest would go to ranked choice voting.

articles.title: The Trump administration is diverting billions in health funding away from low-income countries, defying Congress’ plans
articles.summary: The Trump administration plans to redirect or withhold nearly all funding that Congress had slated for international family planning aid this year – about $6...
articles.body:
The Trump administration plans to redirect or withhold nearly all funding that Congress had slated for international family planning aid this year – about $605 million – according to an internal US State Department budget report and a memo to lawmakers that were obtained by CNN.

The budget plans also involve an effort to move nearly a billion dollars into a global health innovation fund benefiting US corporations, while sharply cutting global health funding for low- and middle-income countries.

The actions have drawn criticism from nonprofit organizations and lawmakers who argue it represents overreach by the administration, given that Congress holds the power to decide how money is spent.

A copy of the budget report – called the preliminary Fiscal Year 2026 allocation – reveals plans to divert or repurpose almost all of the $607.5 million in funding that Congress had allocated to supply contraception and other reproductive health services to women overseas.

Tens of millions of that funding will be diverted to support the "energy security needs" of US partners facing market disruptions amid the wars in Iran and Ukraine, according to a separate memo signed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in September. The memo offered few additional details on how that money would be spent.

For decades, US family planning aid has provided millions of women overseas with modern contraceptives to give them the ability to prevent or space out pregnancies, which research shows improves maternal mortality rates, family incomes and babies' health.

In fiscal year 2024 – before Trump came back to office – US investment in global family planning is estimated to have prevented 34,000 maternal deaths , according to the Guttmacher Institute.

The budget plans also reveal steep reductions in US health assistance for most countries when compared to 2024 funding levels, according to an analysis of the leaked budget document conducted by Public Citizen, a nonprofit consumer advocacy organization. Their analysis, which was shared exclusively with CNN ahead of its publication Saturday, was conducted in conjunction with the nonprofit organizations Partners In Health (PIH) and Population Action International (PAI), a reproductive rights advocacy organization.

The countries with the largest funding decreases for health programs are South Africa, Tanzania and Zimbabwe, which have all been hit with more than $100 million in cuts. Eight countries – Afghanistan, Central African Republic, Gambia, South Africa, Somalia, Sudan, Timor-Leste and Yemen – have had their health funding cut to zero since 2024.

Asked about the funding diversions, a State Department spokesman told CNN that "the administration is consistently evaluating the use of foreign assistance to ensure it is used to meet critical needs, including unanticipated contingencies such as the current global energy crisis, within the context of its annual appropriated budget and the authorities available to the president and the secretary."

Asked about the department's diversions of family planning funding, the spokesman said: "Our focus is on implementing life-saving care, including in HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and maternal and child health, through new, landmark bilateral global health MOUs (memoranda of understanding)."

Vincent Lin, associate director of health policy and advocacy at PIH, told CNN that the latest budget moves are "counter to what Congress has put in the appropriations bills."

"To see dollars that have been fought for and written into the law by Congress moved away or siphoned away to energy security needs, or to US private companies with a profit margin, or out of really important public health programs … I think it is devastating to see that happen," Lin said.

"The executive branch is flagrantly not spending the money that Congress has written into law for a very specific purpose," Lin told CNN. "On the family planning side … this is the clearest situation of the executive branch ignoring and or violating the Congressional will."

In the last two years, the State Department has made several efforts to assume more control over US global health funding and make spending reductions, including by not transferring certain funds to the Centers for Disease Control. CNN has also previously reported on the administration's redirection of $1.35 billion in funding intended for global health programs to cover the cost of closing the US Agency for International Development (USAID).

Many of those changes have lacked public announcements or transparency.

Public Citizen has sued the State Department in an effort to force the release of records surrounding those bilateral global health agreements, which the administration has largely kept confidential. That lawsuit is ongoing in federal court, but some of the documents have been released following Freedom of Information Act requests by watchdog groups.

Congresswoman Lois Frankel (D-FL), who serves on the House Appropriations Committee, said: "The Trump administration's refusal to spend Congressionally-appropriated funds for international family planning, as required by law, is shameful and dangerous."

"These decisions have real, life-changing consequences for women's health, economic security, and opportunities, as well as the well-being of their families and communities," Frankel said in a statement to CNN.

Family planning aid diverted for 'energy security needs'

In a memo to Congress signed by Secretary of State Rubio – which was obtained by CNN and first reported on by The New York Times – he said he authorized the redirection of up to $125 million in foreign aid to support "energy security needs."

More than $48 million of that would be taken from family planning aid, according to the memo.

The memo also spelled out multi-million-dollar diversions away from other US programs, including peacebuilding initiatives between Palestinians and Israelis and overseas assistance for civilian victims of war.

In the memo, Rubio invoked a law that allows the government to use existing foreign assistance funds to address unanticipated crises, saying that funding would be used to "support exigent energy security needs for partners facing coercive supply cutoffs, market disruptions, and inflated costs – particularly due to the deliberate, extortionary actions of Russia, China, and Iran."

It comes as the war in Iran has disrupted energy markets and led to a huge increase in global oil prices .

The State Department memo didn't give further details on how the money diverted for energy security would be spent.

A Democratic Congressional aide told CNN the funding diversion is "an authority that they do have, but it is unlike it's ever been used before."

Separately, the State Department budget document shows that another $32 million originally allocated for the United Nations Population Fund is also being diverted into other health programs.

And a further $524 million in family planning aid is being withheld without a justification given, according to the analysis by Public Citizen, PIH and PAI. That funding is listed in the State Department budget document as "To Be Programmed." Other publicly available budget documents list that sum as "unallocated," which analysts said suggests the funds have not been made available for spending.

"This decision is not consistent with the congressional history of bipartisan support for family planning and reproductive health care," said Nabeeha Kazi Hutchins, president and chief executive of PAI. "It is Congress that holds the power of the purse, and the actions of this administration and the statements of this administration raise very serious concerns about whether the executive branch is exceeding its constitutional authority."

"For us, this is not just an isolated budgetary decision," she told CNN. "This is part of a much broader policy direction that's increasingly restricting women's health and wellbeing."

It's not the first time the Trump administration has indicated it does not plan to spend money on family planning or reproductive health aid, despite the bipartisan allocations made by Congress. Last year, Rubio said in his testimony before the House Committee on Appropriations that with regards to family planning programs, "we're not going to be in that business globally."

The Trump administration has also previously conflated certain kinds of contraception with abortion – something that medical professionals have refuted .

Shifting money into 'innovation fund' as foreign countries hit with aid cuts

The 2026 budget document also showed plans to move $888 million of global health funding into an "innovation fund" that backs US companies working in science, technology and medicine.

At the same time, more than $1.6 billion is being cut from global health funding for foreign countries, according to the analysis by Public Citizen, PIH and PAI.

The move comes after the Trump administration last year launched an overhaul of the way the United States provides health assistance throughout the world, called the "America First Global Health Strategy." The stated goal of the strategy is to have aid recipient countries further develop their own health systems – and the US decrease its assistance spending.

But Public Citizen, PIH and PAI argue that in reality, the funding cuts and diversions are making it more difficult for countries to bolster their own health systems.

"The administration's cuts to country level programming takes away resources that support local health systems and services that deliver care and stop diseases from spreading. The simultaneous increase in resources for the innovation fund prioritizes commercial interests over these fundamental global health objectives," the three organizations said in their analysis.

The administration's justification of the new "America first" strategy was that NGOs were wasting money and it should go directly to foreign governments instead, according to Peter Maybarduk, who directs Public Citizen's initiative on access to medicines. "But the reality is, we're going to take money from the governments and the NGOs and give it to big corporations," he said.

Public Citizen's report also raised concerns about a lack of transparency regarding how government contracts will be awarded through the "innovation fund" of $888 million, which is far more money than when the fund was first created in 2025.

The administration originally set aside $60 million for the innovation fund, according to FY 2025 budget documents.

"The State Department has not clarified how it will solicit and review awards under the (innovation) fund," wrote Public Citizen, PIH and PAI in their report, which also criticized the department for "increasingly relying on non-competitive sole-source awards."

The State Department spokesman told CNN: "The Trump administration is continuing to explore ways to identify and leverage American innovations to save lives, and to do so more cost-effectively while working with Congress."

The department did not respond to CNN's question regarding the specific process for awarding contracts through the innovation fund.

CNN has previously reported on the Trump administration's use of no-bid contracts in other areas of government, particularly surrounding the renovation and construction projects in Washington, DC.

There has been little public information about the specific projects and companies that the global health innovation fund will go towards. However, the State Department has recently announced some partnerships that it says promote American innovation, including contracts with the drone delivery company Zipline, the pharmaceutical company Gilead Sciences and SC Johnson.

"Without a transparent and accountable process for new awards, funding could flow not to those with the best proposals for public health impact, but to those with direct, private access to the administration," the Public Citizen report said. "Moreover, new technologies are not a substitute for direct support to countries."

articles.summary: El periodista analiza las posibles consecuencias de la ausencia de VOX en 'The Wild Project'
articles.body: El periodista Jordi Évole ha analizado la ausencia del líder de VOX, Santiago Abascal, en la serie de entrevistas que ha realizado el youtuber Jordi Wild en 'The Wild Project'. El productor de 'Salvados' ha reflexionado sobre las consecuencias en la aritmética electoral de la decisión de no acudir a la cita. "Dicen las encuestas que nada le pasa factura a VOX. No lo sé Rick. La espantá de Abascal con Jordi Wild va a servir para calibrar el daño o el beneficio que te puede acarrear una decisión así en estos tiempos acelerados de comunicación política", ha publicado en sus redes sociales. Jordi Évole ha considerado que el movimiento de VOX y de Santiago Abascal puede calibrar la relevancia de los denominados nuevos medios, como en el caso de YouTube, en unas elecciones. "Va a determinar si las nuevas formas de comunicación son tan importantes como parece", ha explicado el catalán. El periodista ha compartido en su cuenta personal de X un artículo suyo, publicado en La Vanguardia, en el que analiza en profundidad la ausencia de Abascal en 'The Wild Project'. "Supongo que cuando ya se ve ganador uno se lo piensa dos veces antes de jugársela. para los de Abascal, ir a ser entrevistado a 'The Wild Project' con Jordi Wild, era un riesgo innecesario", ha afirmado Jordi Évole, en referencia a las buenas sensaciones con las que el líder de VOX acabó tras la entrevista con David Broncano en 'La Revuelta'. El catalán también se ha mostrado sorprendido por la actitud personal de Santiago Abascal a la hora de acudir a determinadas entrevistas. "Un señor aparentemente tan testosterónico, tan 'echao p'alante', que ha hablado con tanto desprecio de 'la derechita cobarde', y que ahora se convierte en la 'ultraderechita cobarde'. Curioso", ha insistido Jordi Évole en el artículo del citado medio.

articles.title: Greene calls Duffy, Mullin press briefing ‘a shakedown for more money’
articles.summary: Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) accused Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin of using Friday’s nationwide ground stop to demand more taxpayer money, calling their joint press conference “unreal bulls—.” “It doesn’t matter to any of them that the US Congress and every administration has spent like $15 trillion on…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) accused Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin of using Friday’s nationwide ground stop to demand more taxpayer money, calling their joint press conference “unreal bulls—.”

“It doesn’t matter to any of them that the US Congress and every administration has spent like $15 trillion on foreign wars over the past 25 years but yeah you guys gotta fork over 50 billion more dollars so they can finally fix something in America,” Greene wrote in a post to the social platform X.

Representatives for the Department of Transportation and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. flights Friday afternoon, a rare move used previously in 2023, and before that, as a response to the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.

The FAA cited a “temporary telecommunications outage,” which Duffy said was caused by a system “overloaded with data” that forced them to shut it down.

In the press conference, Duffy said he wanted $50 billion in funding for modernizing the air traffic control system — a key priority of his as transportation secretary.

“I want $50 billion,” Duffy said. “Let’s finish this job: new hardware, new software, new telecommunication.”

While Mullin said there was no indication of a cyberattack or anything nefarious, he said they would not rule anything out. Greene claimed they were lying and that it was “obviously” a cyberattack, without evidence.

The FAA recently rolled out an AI-powered air traffic control tool, called the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) program. The tool debuted first in the Washington, D.C. area and cost the department $875 million.

Air Space Intelligence, the company behind SMART, issued a statement Friday night denying any link to the ground stop, which Duffy echoed during the briefing.

The transportation secretary shared his message to members of Congress requesting increased funding.

“Give President Trump — give Duffy the money. Let them finish this job so we don’t have to do a press conference at 8:30 at night ever again,” Duffy said.

articles.body:
U.S. airports and airlines are still playing catch up on Saturday following Friday’s four hour long nationwide ground, with travelers across the country scrambling to get to their destinations after facing delays and cancellations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday night he expects the transition back to normal air travel to be “slow” following the rare grounding, which he attributed to a data overload and outdated air traffic control systems.

While members of his cabinet took the podium to discuss the Federal Aviation Administration’s move, President Trump stayed silent on the stoppage throughout Friday afternoon. He has no public events scheduled over the weekend.

Meanwhile, the Federalist Society — a conservative legal organization — is convening in Washington for the second day of its annual “National Lawyers Convention.” During its opening night, Secretary of State Marco Rubio took the stage, adopting an optimistic tone of American idealism amid buzz surrounding his alleged interest in launching a presidential campaign. The Hill’s Laura Kelly has more .

Meanwhile, several midterm races have yet to be called over a week out from Election Day — including the contentious Alaska Senate race between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) and Democrat Mary Peltola.
