articles.title: Florida Republican on Democrats' strategy: 'That's the choice they have to make...persecution or policy'
articles.summary: Controversial Florida congressman charges Democrats will choose to pursue persecution over policy, but also signals willingness to compromise, given the right conditions.
articles.body: Florida's Rep. Randy Fine has a blunt prescription for a House Republican conference staring down a steep Democratic majority in January: stop worrying about compromise, hand the minority gavel to Rep. Jim Jordan, and start fighting, suggesting that Democrats will likely pursue political persecution as the main focus in the next Congress. In a wide-ranging interview with Fox News Digital, Fine—who expanded his own victory margin to 19 points even as Republicans lost control of the chamber—argued that voters punished the GOP not for its policies, but because they didn't see lawmakers willing to go to the mat for them. ‘HE BLAMED THE JEWS’: GOP CONGRESSMAN LEVELS EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATION AGAINST JD VANCE OVER ELECTION POSTMORTEM For Fine, the message sent by Jordan's election is unambiguous: "Well, it says to me that we're ready to fight back. I mean, Jim Jordan has two unique qualifications for the job. "One, he's our best fighter. He protected and fought for President Trump during the ridiculous impeachments of President Trump's first term. He's just somebody who knows how to go into the arena and fight back. "But the second thing is, he's an extraordinary communicator. And over the next two years, we are in a very diminished minority. That's going to be our greatest strength, is to point out why the Democratic policies won't actually improve anyone's lives, and to point out the policies that we would propose that will. So, as a fighter and a communicator, I think he's very well positioned to lead us for the next two years." Fine downplays policy as the primary driver of the disastrous 2026 blue tsunami: "I don't know that we need to change our policies. And I don't even know how much of our messaging we need to change. What we need to do is we need to fight. I believe that we lost the election because voters thought we didn't care about their problems, because they didn't see us fighting to solve them. "Voters will vote for you if they see you fighting, even if you fail. But they won't vote for you if they don't see you fighting. Now I'm a guy who defied the odds. I increased my margin in the election. I may be the only Republican in the country to do that. I won my last election by 14, I won this one by 19." With House Republicans shifting from passing bills to playing defense after electing Rep. Jim Jordan to succeed outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson as minority leader, Fine drew a sharp line between the two leadership roles. "Well, it's a very different job. Look, I think if we kept the majority, I think Mike Johnson would still be the speaker. The speaker's job and the minority leader's job are completely different. So Mike Johnson's job for the next 50 plus days is to try to get as many good things passed through the House as he can. FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM' "Jim Jordan's not going to be able to pass anything. The Democrats could have a 90 to 100 vote majority. His job is going to be to fight back when they're impeaching and they're interrogating and they are being vindictive, but also again to communicate why their policies will not make people's lives better. "They're going to come out and say Medicare for all. We're going to have to say, 'No, no there's no such thing. It's going to be Medicaid for all. When you give it to everyone, everyone will suffer. We'll end up like Canada where there are death panels or the UK where you can wait a year or two to get to a doctor.' That's what we're going to have to do: fight back and communicate. That's a very different job than what Mike Johnson had to do the last two years." Gridlock may be the persistent feature of the next Congress, but Fine does not completely discard the potential for compromise: "Well, first off, compromise isn't inevitable. We may not do very much for the next two years. And I think that's the most likely outcome. Democrats pass ridiculous things, President Trump vetoes them, and then we uphold the veto in the House and the Senate. I think that's the most likely outcome for the next two years. "If it relates to compromise, you have to see what we're offered. So, for example, if Democrats would agree to voter ID, which is a huge thing the American people want, they might be able to extract a concession from us. If they're willing to stop so much of the ridiculous immigration into this country, they might be able to get concessions from us on other things. So, the problem is this: to Democrats, compromise means we give them what they want. It's always a one-way street. "It's funny, when Democrats win, they say elections have consequences. When we win, they say we need to be bipartisan. And that's how their viewpoint is. They never come to our side of the world. So I'll see if they want to compromise. I'll be open to it. But it will truly require us getting some of the things that we want that they have fought us on for the time I've been in Congress." On foreign policy objectives, Fine points to several Democrats he's prepared to work with, while clarifying his position on Israel: "Sure. I mean, look, in the Senate, you've got John Fetterman, who I think is an incredibly strong advocate for Western civilization. I don't think it's fair to say I'm an advocate for Israel. That makes it sound like I'm just an advocate for a country. It's more than that. "The United States and Israel are the only two countries in the world that are unambiguously standing up to Muslim terror, which seeks to fundamentally redefine life for all of us around the world. So I'm on the side of Western civilization and John Fetterman embodies that in the Senate. I think you've got guys like Jared Moskowitz and Josh Gottheimer on the House side, on the Democratic side, who do as well…Unfortunately, I think they're pretty outnumbered at this point, but if they want to fight with me, I'm happy to fight alongside them." Finally, Fine contends that the Democrats face a clear dichotomy in how they want to proceed to govern, but argues they will likely make the wrong choice: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The American people elected Democrats not because they wanted investigations and persecution. They elected Democrats because they didn't think we were solving their problems. If they make the mistake of going down the vengeance and persecution path, they'll end up in two years just the same way we did. If they try to solve the problems of the American people, they'll do well. "The problem is their ideas don't work. Remember, the Affordable Care Act didn't make health care affordable. But if they try to do things that will help the American people, at least they'll be listening to them. But that's the choice they have to make. Persecution or policy. I think they're going to choose persecution, but we'll find out in a couple of months."

articles.title: Anti-Trump Republican courts other defectors as House weighs another vote against Iran war
articles.summary: Thomas Massie says he's offering Republicans a "life boat from MAGA" as he pushes a new Iran War Powers resolution to the House floor soon..
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: House Republicans and Democrats are preparing another effort to challenge President Donald Trump's military operations in Iran, with lawmakers signaling that additional Republicans could break with the president and support a War Powers resolution. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told Fox News Digital that another Iran War Powers resolution could come to the House floor "in the next few legislative days" or around Christmas. This would mark the fourth attempt this year to restrict Trump's military actions against Iran. "I'm offering Republicans a life boat from MAGA," Massie told Fox News Digital, expressing optimism that more members of his party could join the effort. 7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS House Armed Services Committee Chairman Mike Rogers, R-Ala., told Fox News Digital that he would oppose the resolution but acknowledged that "Massie has been having conversations with members" in an effort to secure additional Republican support. Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., echoed Rogers' assessment, suggesting that "one or two" additional Republicans could join Massie and the Democrats who previously supported the measure. SWING-DISTRICT REPUBLICAN BREAKS WITH TRUMP, PUSHES LIMITS ON IRAN WAR Reps. Tom Barrett, R-Mich., Warren Davidson, R-Ohio, and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., previously voted in favor of an Iran War Powers resolution. Barrett told Fox News Digital on Thursday that he would maintain his support if the new resolution mirrors the previous legislation. "My position would be consistent for it," Barrett said. However, Barrett expressed skepticism that additional Republicans would join the effort, noting that few members appeared willing to shift their positions during the previous vote. GOP HOLDS WITH TRUMP ON IRAN WAR, BUT CRACKS EMERGE AS DEADLINE NEARS Massie also acknowledged uncertainty over whether he could secure more Republican votes, criticizing his party's continued support for Trump's military operations. "Congress is paralyzed," Massie told Fox News Digital, accusing Republicans of remaining "still in the suicide pact with this administration." TRUMP SUFFERS RARE HOUSE DEFEAT AS BIPARTISAN VOTE MOVES TO WITHDRAW TROOPS FROM IRAN CONFLICT House Democrats, meanwhile, expressed optimism that Republicans' losses in the 2026 midterm elections could encourage more GOP lawmakers to break with Trump's foreign policy agenda. "If they're listening to the people that sent them here, yes," Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., told Fox News Digital when asked whether additional Republicans could support the effort. "That's what they should do." Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., also expressed confidence that more Republicans could join the effort, saying she "thinks they would." Meanwhile, Rep. Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz., suggested that Republicans may feel less pressure to remain aligned with Trump following the midterm elections — especially as many prepare to leave Congress and others hunker down to serve in the minority. "The threat of Trump dumping a lot of money into Republican districts is over, perhaps more members of Congress we think represent their communities will listen to what constituents are saying about the war," Grijalva told Fox News Digital. TRUMP PLEDGES TO VETO 'INSANE' DEM BILLS, PINPOINTS ISSUE PARTIALLY TO BLAME FOR REPUBLICAN LOSSES The renewed effort comes as lawmakers continue debating Congress' constitutional authority over military operations and the president's ability to conduct sustained hostilities without congressional authorization. Under the Constitution, Congress holds the power to declare war, while the president serves as commander in chief of the armed forces. The War Powers Resolution of 1973 establishes procedures and limits for military operations conducted without congressional authorization. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Despite growing discussions among lawmakers, no vote on an Iran War Powers resolution has been scheduled or confirmed.

articles.title: Democrats win an election and immediately move to subvert democracy
articles.summary: The standard for impeachment is not “kind of legalizing a lot.”
articles.body:
It appears democracy is too important to be left to voters.

After Democrats ran on “saving democracy” from its imminent destruction, many voters may be a bit confused by the actions of their newly elected representatives. Democratic politicians and pundits are moving to negate certain results in the last election and to circumvent future votes on key reforms. The country could soon be experiencing the greatest changes to our constitutional system in 250 years, but the public will have little to say about it.

In Seattle, socialist Mayor Katie Wilson announced that she and the city would move to block a statewide initiative approved by 36 of 39 counties. The public voted to require the separation of boys and girls in K-12 sports. It is an issue that has overwhelming support among both Democrats and Republicans, with polls showing roughly 70 percent of Americans supporting girls’ sports for girls alone.

But Wilson and others do not like the decision, so they are seeking to protect the public from their supposedly bad choices.

In Colorado, Governor-elect Phil Weiser (D), the former dean at the University of Colorado Law School, was a prominent figure in the “No Kings” protests before the election. But after his election, he decided that the voters’ democratic decisions on transgender policies were inherently flawed and he would have to correct them.

Colorado voters passed a ban on male athletes in girls and women’s sports. Proposition 134 defined girls as having female reproductive organs and boys as having male reproductive organs. So that there would be no ambiguity later, the drafters expressly added that “students assigned male at birth play only on boys teams or co-ed teams and vice versa for females.”

The public also passed Proposition 135, banning gender-affirming surgeries for minors.

Weiser, however, declared that, with a new supermajority in both houses, Democrats would “have to take a look at these anti-trans measures … to fix [them] and provide a much more human and sound approach.”

This is the same politician who recently insisted that he was “defending democracy” and standing for “our government of the people, by the people, and for the people.” But apparently, the last thing large-D Democrats want to do is actually listen to the people.

The “saving democracy” crowd seems to have a very serious problem with democracy.

In Alaska, the champions of democracy who supported Alaska Democratic Senatorial nominee Mary Peltola (D) worked to put a decoy “Dan Sullivan” on the ballot with the sole aim of confusing voters. The New York Times reported in painful detain that the effort had been coordinated at the highest level of the Democratic establishment, including the involvement of the law group of Marc Elias, the notorious lawyer involved in the Steele Dossier controversy .

In the prior election, many of these same figures supported efforts to prevent voters from voting for Trump and other Republicans — requiring the Supreme Court to step in and restore to the ballot the candidate who went on to win the popular vote.

Democrats are now planning to fundamentally change the constitutional system. As one Harvard law professor explained it, these committed democracy-defenders will guarantee that Republicans “never win another election.” The key is to prevent voters from actually voting on any of the changes.

Democratic leaders are openly talking about packing the Supreme Court to allow an array of changes by judicial fiat. Although many Americans still oppose court packing, this could technically be done by a vote of Congress.

There is also a building effort to effectively abolish the Electoral College , to increase the power of high-population blue states without actually seeking a constitutional amendment. Securing the White House after negating the Electoral College would mean that many of these changes could be accomplished by a simple majority vote.

There is also an effort to simply declare the District of Columbia a state, without a constitutional amendment to alter the status of D.C. as a federal enclave and non-state in Article I, Section 8. (Democrats are also seeking to add Puerto Rico, to give Democrats an even greater edge in the Senate.) Past polls show considerable opposition to making a state out of the federal district whose current boundaries were carved out of Maryland’s territory.

The key is to make these changes through Washington rather than giving citizens a vote on such fundamental changes. A packed court alone would bring radical changes, particularly with Democrats pointing to far-left Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson as their model for the new stacked court.

This has long been a pattern for far-left political movements. In my book “ Rage and the Republic ,” I discuss how the French radicals called the Jacobins took power by marshaling the rage of the people, but then ruled the nation as a small elite. While espousing faith in the “general will” of the people, the Jacobins concentrated power in the hands of brutal committees with such blood-soaked figures as Maximilien Robespierre.

The Jacobins used the language of popular government to assume power, but not to share it with the people. While we have a representative democracy, the Framers still wanted citizens to approve major changes to our system. Today the new Jacobins are seeking structural changes to guarantee their own power while offering the voters ways to vent their rage rather than play a role in governance.

Taking another page from the Jacobins, Democratic leaders are promising heads. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) promised “many, many, many investigations” into what she calls the “criminals” of the opposing party. She even recently suggested that conservative Supreme Court justices might be impeached for ruling against the wishes of her party.

“I mean, of course, this Supreme Court as well has also kind of legalized a lot of his criminality,” she said. Of course, the standard for impeachment is not “kind of legalizing a lot.” But that is just the standard in the Constitution, which is itself becoming increasingly irrelevant to the Democratic Party’s agenda.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “ Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution .”
